result.headline: Bengaluru households get undated, round-number scrap prices: about half the mill price for newspaper (₹10/kg against roughly ₹20/kg) and about a sixth of the exchange price for aluminium cans (₹60/kg against MCX ₹347.50/kg on 28 Sep 2026). Exchange prices can't be republished without MCX or LME licences, so Luma.Green should build its price board from its own verified rate cards and trades.

findings.point: The prices households see are static round numbers with no date, while the materials underneath move daily (metals) or weekly (paper).
findings.detail: The Kabadiwala's Bangalore page lists newspaper at ₹10/kg, carton ₹3, PET ₹10, aluminium ₹150 and beverage cans ₹60/kg. No update date is shown, and each city has its own page. Kabadiwala Online (Delhi NCR) gives ranges (newspaper ₹12–18, aluminium ₹95–130), calls them indicative, says metal rates follow the exchanges every day, and has a ₹999 minimum pickup. scraprates.in quotes Bengaluru newspaper at a precise-looking ₹13.69/kg (28 Sep 2026), calls it a dealer 'wholesale baseline', does not explain how it is calculated, and says household pickup quotes run ₹5–7/kg lower. It also says free doorstep pickup usually needs 25–50 kg.

findings.point: Metal benchmarks move every trading day and are published to the rupee; this is where the gap to the household price is widest.
findings.detail: On 28 Sep 2026 MCX aluminium was ₹347.50/kg (−0.4% from ₹349.05) and LME aluminium was US$3,268/t (+0.6%). NALCO's list price for aluminium ingots was ₹367–379/kg on 19 Sep 2026. BigMint publishes daily Indian scrap assessments with the day's change, e.g. melting scrap delivered to Mandi Gobindgarh at ₹42,600/t, up ₹1,000 (+2.4%).

findings.point: Waste-paper prices move in weekly steps, with occasional double-digit swings inside two to three weeks.
findings.detail: Feb 2024: domestic waste paper fell about 20% in 9–10 days (₹19.50 to ₹15.50–16/kg) when kraft and duplex demand dried up. Jul 2023: it rose ₹1.5–2.5/kg in about 20 days, driven by import prices and monsoon disruption to collection. Jan 2025: corrugated waste (OCC) rose ₹2,000/t to ₹20,500/t in North India as collection fell 55–60%. Freight, mill demand, monsoon and festivals all move the price.

findings.point: Bengaluru's own value-chain study prices every layer. For newspaper, the price rose about ₹1/kg per step, and households got roughly 67–71% of the mill price.
findings.detail: The BBMP study 'Extracting Value from Bengaluru's Dry Waste Chain' (Nov 2014) found: kabadiwala paid ₹10/kg, large aggregators ₹11 (transport about ₹1/kg extra), traders ₹12–13 (₹1 margin), paper mills in Hosur, Sivakasi, Coimbatore and Bengaluru ₹14–15 delivered. Bengaluru produced 8,000–9,000 t of newspaper a month. Jolly Mohalla (Cottonpet) was the wholesale hub. Cartons: kabadiwala ₹6–7, aggregator ₹8–8.50, traders +₹1–1.50. DWCC price lists (17 Sep 2013) paid ₹7–8 for newspaper and ₹15 for PET.

findings.point: For aluminium cans and PET the gap between household and factory is two to six times, and for cans it seems to have widened since 2014.
findings.detail: 2014 Bengaluru can chain: DWCC ₹35, kabadiwala ₹45, aggregator ₹60, recycler ₹110, billets sold at ₹120/kg. The kabadiwala price was about 38% of the billet price. PET went from ₹15–18/kg at the kabadiwala to ₹45–50 at dispatch to recyclers in Gujarat and Mumbai. 2026: The Kabadiwala pays ₹60/kg for cans in Bengaluru, about 17% of MCX aluminium (₹347.50). Used-beverage-can (UBC) lots on IndiaMART (Delhi sellers' asking prices) are ₹120–290/kg, mostly ₹145–230. Bengaluru utensil aluminium is ₹215–220/kg and extrusion ₹225–310/kg. The 2014 and 2026 figures come from different kinds of sources, so the comparison shows direction, not a precise change.

findings.point: A 2026 snapshot for newspaper in Bengaluru shows households get roughly 35–50% of the price of mill-grade lots.
findings.detail: Households: ₹10/kg (The Kabadiwala), or about ₹7–9 if pickup quotes really run ₹5–7 below scraprates' ₹13.69 baseline. Bengaluru newspaper sellers on IndiaMART mostly ask ₹12–20/kg (outliers of ₹9 and ₹95 are special grades). Mixed ONP for paper mills is offered at ₹20/kg with a 5 t minimum (Mumbai seller). All marketplace figures are asking prices, not completed trades.

findings.point: Prices differ by city even on the same app, and southern paper mills pay less, so every price table must be per city.
findings.detail: The Kabadiwala pays less in Bengaluru than in Delhi: carton ₹3 vs ₹6, cans ₹60 vs ₹70, newspaper ₹10 vs ₹11, copper ₹500 vs ₹550, brass ₹400 vs ₹450. Aluminium (₹150) and PET (₹10) are the same in both cities. In Jul 2023 southern mills paid ₹13–13.5/kg for kraft waste against ₹15.8–16.5 in Meerut and Muzaffarnagar. Where material goes also varies by type: Bengaluru paper goes to mills in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, aluminium is recycled locally (Nayandahalli, Kumbalgodu, Harohalli), and PET travels to Gujarat and Mumbai.

findings.point: Licences limit what Luma.Green can show from exchanges: MCX allows only delayed data on public websites under an agreement, and LME needs a paid licence for any public website or app.
findings.detail: MCX: showing its data needs a real-time or delayed feed subscription and an MCX agreement. Public websites may show delayed data only. Resale in any form is banned. Public internet display needs explicit MCX permission. The internet feed costs ₹1,00,000 + tax a year before product charges. LME: showing LME data on a public website or app needs a distribution licence: US$25,000 a year for real-time or 30-minute-delayed data, or a one-off US$4,000 for next-day data. Prices calculated from LME data (LME calls these 'reference values') may also need a separate derived-data licence.

findings.point: Professional price reporters build trusted indices from confirmed trades with a public method. Luma.Green's board can copy that pattern at city level.
findings.detail: BigMint runs 800+ price assessments in 40+ countries. It builds them from confirmed transactions and market-checked deals, has its method externally audited against IOSCO standards (the international securities regulators' body), uses SEBI-certified analysts, invites firms to submit prices, and sells redistribution rights through data licences. It covers scrap, polymers and non-ferrous metals, but not household-level prices.

findings.point: B2B marketplaces already sell 'one fair live price' to businesses; the household and city level is still open.
findings.detail: Recykal.Market claims 10K+ verified GST-registered businesses, 3M+ tonnes traded, ₹2,500 Cr+ in value across 28+ states and UTs. It promises one transparent rate with no brokers or haggling. It does not publish a household-level city price board.

findings.point: Indian regulators already use floor-and-ceiling price bands in recycling markets, which supports admin floors but also shows they get challenged.
findings.detail: The E-Waste (Management) Amendment Rules 2024 (notified 8 Mar 2024) make the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) set the highest and lowest prices for trading e-waste recycling certificates (EPR certificates) at 100% and 30% of the penalty for missing EPR targets. Experts raised concerns about oversight and possible manipulation of set prices.

findings.point: Karnataka's scrap trade has recent large-scale fake-trade fraud, so prices built from trades must require proof that goods physically moved.
findings.detail: On 16 May 2026 Karnataka's Commercial Taxes Department exposed 127 bogus 'scrap' firms with ₹2,384 crore of fake turnover and about ₹420 crore of fraudulent GST input credit. The firms used circular invoices without warehouses, staff or transport records; one firm's reported turnover grew from ₹50 crore to ₹945 crore in three years.

findings.point: Shops learn prices from the next buyer up the chain, day by day, and traders earn their margin partly by providing credit.
findings.detail: The BBMP study found the local scrap dealer sets each day's price from market demand. Dealers with manual balers get better prices. Traders, many with direct tie-ups to processors, pay sellers in cash immediately but wait to be paid by processors, and take the largest margin in the chain. This makes the case for a public daily price and, later, faster settlement between businesses.

recommendations.feature: Public Bengaluru price board at /prices/bengaluru and /prices/bengaluru/{material}, in all 12 languages and indexed by search engines. Each material shows the price range households get, a typical price, the 7-day change, a Live or Guide status, how many shops and pickups it is based on, the update time, and a WhatsApp share image. Every number carries a visible 'Sample data' badge until real data flows.
recommendations.why: Nobody publishes a dated, sourced household price for Bengaluru: apps show undated round numbers and scraprates.in shows unexplained two-decimal figures. A board with honest ranges and freshness labels is the clearest thing to show investors, and 'scrap rate today' pages are something people already look for.

recommendations.feature: A 'Where your rupee goes' chart for newspaper and aluminium cans (household → shop → yard → mill or recycler), each step labelled with its source and date.
recommendations.why: The gap is the investor story. In 2014 Bengaluru newspaper went ₹10 → ₹11 → ₹12–13 → ₹14–15. Today a household gets ₹60/kg for cans against MCX aluminium at ₹347.50/kg, about 17%.

recommendations.feature: Admin price console (/admin/prices). Floors and fallbacks per city and material with effective dates, CSV paste for bulk edits, a plausible-price band per material, suggested values (fallback = 28-day median; floor = 75% of fallback, rounded down to ₹0.50; at most 10% change a week without a written reason), and every change in the audit log.
recommendations.why: Data has to be easy to change, and ADR 0008 already makes the admin own the floor and fallback tables. Suggested values and bands stop one-off mistakes like a stray ₹25/kg newspaper rate.

recommendations.feature: A daily price calculation (06:00 IST) from an append-only log of every price input. It takes one value per business (completed trades weigh 1.0; rate cards and admin survey quotes weigh 0.5), merges related businesses into one, drops the obvious outliers, uses the weighted median, and marks a price Live only when at least 3 independent businesses report, at least one with a trade. Daily moves above ±10% (paper and plastic) or ±5% (metals) are held until the admin confirms.
recommendations.why: Price reporters like BigMint build on confirmed trades with a published method. With only a handful of pilot testers, the minimum count and the Guide fallback stop thin data being shown as 'live'.

recommendations.feature: Freshness rules and reminders. Paper and plastic rate cards count as fresh for 14 days, metal rate cards for 7. Kabadiwalas get a one-tap 'Are your prices still right?' SMS or WhatsApp before a card goes stale, and stale cards drop out of the board. The admin sees a banner if the floor and fallback tables go 10 days without review.
recommendations.why: Metals move every trading day and paper can swing 20% in 10 days (Feb 2024). Rate cards that never change would underpay households or cause losses for kabadiwalas.

recommendations.feature: Honour-rate and anti-manipulation checks. Compare each shop's posted rate with what its receipts actually paid. A trade counts only if it was weighed, confirmed by both sides (the household by SMS code) and has a payment method recorded; yard trades also need a weighbridge slip photo. Merge related accounts (same phone, GSTIN, PAN or UPI ID) and exclude self-trades and back-and-forth trades.
recommendations.why: Karnataka's ₹2,384 crore fake-invoice scrap case (May 2026) shows circular trading is common. Advertising high prices to win bookings is also a likely trick in the pilot.

recommendations.feature: Yard buy-price posts: each yard posts price per material, minimum lot, loose or baled, and collected or delivered. Posts expire after 7 days and are shown to verified kabadiwalas nearby on the 'My stock' screen. Until enough yards post, the admin phone-surveys at least 3 yards per material each week.
recommendations.why: No free source gives yard buying prices for Bengaluru, and the kabadiwala-to-yard hand-off is 'the most important part'. Marketplace listings are asking prices, not trades.

recommendations.feature: No exchange data in the pilot: no automated feed, no exchange number on screen, and no price tied to an exchange by formula. Each table revision gets a 'market check' note giving the reason and what the admin looked at.
recommendations.why: MCX allows only delayed data on public websites, under an agreement, with no resale. LME needs a US$25,000-a-year licence (or US$4,000 one-off for next-day data), and prices calculated from LME data may need a separate licence.

recommendations.feature: Area-level boards that fall back from area to city to state to national, with an admin city factor for launching new cities. Store each business's location (geohash) now so areas can be split later without a migration.
recommendations.why: The same app pays ₹3 vs ₹6/kg for carton in Bengaluru vs Delhi, and southern mills paid ₹13–13.5 vs ₹15.8–16.5/kg in the north (2023). A national rollout needs area and city pricing without rebuilding the design.

recommendations.feature: A licensed metals reference, taken as a delayed or end-of-day MCX feed through an authorised vendor or under a BigMint data licence, for business dashboards and automatic 'market moved' alerts, after legal review.
recommendations.why: Yards, recyclers and manufacturers price aluminium, copper and brass against exchanges. A licence makes that legal and removes the admin's manual checks.

recommendations.feature: Publish the method, a complaints process and a monthly change log, so the board becomes a citable 'Luma.Green City Scrap Index'. Later, let escrow trades between businesses settle at the board price plus or minus an agreed premium.
recommendations.why: The founders want the industry to adopt the platform's norms. Recognised benchmarks win trust through a public, audited method (BigMint follows IOSCO standards), and a shared settlement price reduces haggling and dependence on traders' credit.

result.artifactMarkdown:
# Luma.Green price engine — spec v0.1 (29 Sep 2026)

**Goal:** one dated, traceable price per city × material × level each day. It uses only data we own, keeps the admin in control, and follows the existing rules: integer paise per kg, integer grams, append-only history.

## 1. Levels
| Level | Who pays whom | When |
|---|---|---|
| L1 | Kabadiwala → household (doorstep or drop-off) | Pilot, public |
| L2 | Yard → kabadiwala (sorted; loose or baled) | Pilot, signed-in kabadiwalas only |
| L3 | Recycler → yard (baled, graded) | Scale |
| L4 | Manufacturer → recycler (flakes, ingot, pulp) | Scale |

## 2. Inputs → `priceObservations` (append-only)
| Tier | Input | Weight | Counts only if |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Pickup receipts (L1); completed yard collections (L2) | 1.0 (0.5 if under 1 kg in the window) | Weighed, confirmed by both sides (household by SMS code), payment method recorded; L2 also needs a weighbridge slip photo |
| T2 | Kabadiwala rate cards (L1); yard buy posts (L2) | 0.5 | Business verified; card fresh (§5) |
| T3 | Admin phone survey (≥3 businesses per material; name and time logged) | 0.5 | ≤7 days old |
| T4 | MCX, LME, price reporters such as BigMint, IndiaMART asking prices | **0** | Admin reads them for judgment only (§8) |

Row fields: `city`, `zone?` (geohash-5), `materialId`, `level`, `paisePerKg`, `grams?`, `source`, `orgId`, `observedAt`, `basis` (pickup or drop-off; loose or baled; ex-GST).

## 3. Admin tables
- Existing: `priceFloors` and `fallbackRates` (city × material, dated). New: `priceBands` — a plausible min and max per material, plus the largest allowed daily move (±10% paper and plastic, ±5% metals).
- The console suggests values; the admin decides. Fallback = 28-day L1 median, rounded down to ₹0.50. Floor = 75% of fallback, rounded down to ₹0.50. Moves over 10% a week need a written reason. Bulk edit by CSV paste; every save writes new rows (`effectiveFrom`, author, reason) and an `auditLog` entry.

## 4. Daily calculation (Convex cron, 06:00 IST; the admin can re-run it)
1. Window: last 7 days, or 14 if fewer than 3 businesses report.
2. Drop rows outside the band, from unverified businesses, self-trades, and back-and-forth trades (the same kg reversed within 48 h). Merge related businesses (same owner phone, GSTIN, PAN or UPI ID) into one.
3. One value per business: the median of its T1 trades if it has any, otherwise its T2 or T3 price.
4. With 4 or more businesses, drop values more than 30% from the median.
5. Typical = weighted median. Range = lowest to highest remaining value. Round to ₹0.50 on screen; store paise.
6. **Live** needs ≥3 independent businesses, at least one with a trade. Otherwise **Guide**: show the fallback price with its review date.
7. Circuit breaker: a move bigger than the band's daily limit keeps yesterday's price until the admin confirms.
8. L1 prices are never shown below the floor.

Output: a `priceBoards` row {city, material, level, lowPaise, typicalPaise, highPaise, nOrgs, nTrades, status, computedAt}.

## 5. Freshness
| Item | Fresh for | Then |
|---|---|---|
| Rate card (paper, plastic) | 14 days | Reminder at day 12; dropped after 30 days |
| Rate card (metals) | 7 days | Reminder at day 6; dropped after 14 days |
| Yard post | 7 days | Expires; one tap to renew |
| Floors and fallbacks | Reviewed weekly | Admin banner at 10 days; the board shows "reviewed on <date>" |

## 6. Anti-manipulation
One vote per business, with related businesses merged. Trades must be proven (§2). Rate cards can change at most 3 times a day. **Honour rate:** if more than 20% of a shop's pickups pay over 5% below its posted card, the card leaves the board and the shop drops in ranking. Admin overrides are logged and shown as "adjusted by admin". Individual shop prices appear only inside a household's booking, never on the public board.

## 7. Regions
Bengaluru city-wide for now. Store each business's geohash. Fallback order: area (≥5 businesses) → city → state → national, and the board says which it used. A new city copies the nearest city's fallback × an admin city factor.

## 8. Index data: licence limits (checked 29 Sep 2026)
| Source | Show publicly? | Use in a formula? |
|---|---|---|
| MCX | Delayed data only, under an MCX agreement; no resale. Feed ₹1,00,000 + tax a year plus product charges | Needs explicit permission |
| LME | Only with a distribution licence: US$25k a year for real-time or 30-min delay; US$4k one-off for next-day | Prices built from LME data may need a derived-data licence |
| Price reporters (BigMint etc.) | Only under a data licence | Same |
| IndiaMART and other apps | No; don't scrape | No; these are asking prices, not trades |
| Our own rate cards, receipts and posts | Yes (our terms say so) | Yes |

**Pilot rule:** no exchange feed, no exchange number on screen, no formula tied to an exchange.

## 9. Public board
`/prices/bengaluru` and `/prices/bengaluru/{material}`: indexed, in 12 languages, cached until the next daily calculation. Each line reads "Households get ₹A–B/kg · typical ₹C · 7-day change · Live/Guide · N shops, N pickups · updated <time>", with a "How we calculate" link and a WhatsApp share image. The prototype shows a **Sample data** badge on every number.

## 10. Worked example: Bengaluru board for 29 Sep 2026
The input rows are **illustrative seed data**. The reference prices are real and dated.

### Newspaper `PAPER-NEWS` (L1)
Admin: floor ₹7.50, fallback ₹10.00 (reference: The Kabadiwala Bangalore ₹10/kg), band ₹5–20, largest daily move ±10%.

| Business | Input | ₹/kg | Weight | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| K1 | Rate card | 10.00 | 0.5 | kept |
| K2 | 6 receipts, 84 kg | 11.00 | 1.0 | kept |
| K3 | 5 receipts, 61 kg | 12.00 | 1.0 | kept |
| K4 | 3 receipts, 40 kg (card ₹12.00) | 11.50 | 1.0 | kept; honour rate 96%, not flagged |
| K5 | Rate card | 25.00 | — | outside band → admin queue |

Weighted median of 10.00 (0.5), 11.00 (1), 11.50 (1), 12.00 (1): total weight 3.5, halfway mark 1.75, reached at **₹11.50**. Range ₹10–12. 4 businesses, 3 with trades → **Live**. Last week ₹11.00 → +4.5%, within the 10% limit.
**Board line:** Newspaper — households get ₹10–12/kg · typical ₹11.50 · ▲4.5% · 4 shops, 14 pickups · Live.
L2: two yards post ₹13.00 (300 kg minimum, yard collects) and ₹13.50 (500 kg, delivered). With only 2 yards, kabadiwalas see them as offers, not as a board price.
Admin reference (not displayed): dealer "baseline" ₹13.69 (scraprates.in, 28 Sep); Bengaluru IndiaMART asking prices ₹12–20; mill-grade ONP ₹20/kg (5 t minimum, Mumbai). The 2014 Bengaluru chain ran ₹10 → ₹11 → ₹12–13 → ₹14–15 at the mill.

### Aluminium cans `METAL-ALU-CAN` (L1)
Admin: floor ₹45, fallback ₹60 (reference: The Kabadiwala Bangalore ₹60/kg), band ₹30–150, largest daily move ±5%, rate cards fresh for 7 days.

| Business | Input | ₹/kg | Weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| K1 | Rate card | 55 | 0.5 |
| K2 | 3 receipts, 1.9 kg | 60 | 1.0 |
| K3 | 1 receipt, 0.6 kg | 60 | 0.5 (under 1 kg) |
| K5 | Rate card | 70 | 0.5 |

Weighted median: total weight 2.5, halfway mark 1.25, reached at **₹60**. Range ₹55–70; every value is within 30% of the median. 4 businesses → **Live**.
**Board line:** Aluminium cans — ₹55–70/kg · typical ₹60 · 4 shops · Live. Show "≈ ₹ per can" only after weighing 100 local cans to set a cans-per-kg factor.
Admin reference (not displayed): MCX aluminium ₹347.50/kg and LME US$3,268/t (28 Sep); NALCO ingot ₹367–379/kg (19 Sep); UBC lots ₹120–290/kg (IndiaMART Delhi asking prices); Bengaluru utensil scrap ₹215–220/kg. A household's ₹60 is about 17% of MCX. In 2014 the Bengaluru chain was ₹45 (shop) → ₹60 (aggregator) → ₹110 (recycler). Metals rule: if exchange prices have moved more than 5% since the last review, re-check the aluminium floor and fallback that week.
risks: The prototype's sample prices could mislead investors if they look live. Put a 'Sample data' badge on every number and keep the seed data separate from real data.

The pilot has only a handful of testers, so most board lines will say 'Guide' for weeks. Plan a weekly admin phone survey of at least 3 yards and shops per material so the board has something to show.

Competition law: a platform-set floor or fallback that competing kabadiwalas all copy could look like coordinated buying prices (the Competition Act 2002, s.3, covers agreements that directly or indirectly fix purchase prices). Get Indian counsel's view. Present floors as household protection and let shops price freely above them.
Licence breach: if developers show MCX, LME or price-reporter numbers publicly, or tie a public price to them by formula, without a licence.
Floors set too high could make kabadiwalas drop materials or refuse pickups, which is the pilot's named failure mode ('pickups unprofitable'). Cap weekly floor changes and watch acceptance rates.
False precision (e.g. ₹13.69) and 'live' labels based on a few data points destroy trust. Round to ₹0.50 on screen and always show how many shops and pickups a price is based on.
Manipulation through related accounts, advertising high rates then paying less, and fake or circular trades, as in Karnataka's ₹2,384 crore scrap-invoice case.

Metals move daily while rate cards change slowly, so households get underpaid when prices rise and kabadiwalas lose when prices fall. Short freshness windows and the circuit breakers limit this but don't remove it.
Disputes at the door if a shop pays less than the board's 'typical' price. Show the range, say the final price depends on weight at the door, and track each shop's honour rate.
Marketplace listings (IndiaMART) are asking prices that mix grades. Never use them as inputs, only as a sanity check.
openQuestions: Will Bengaluru yards post buy prices on the platform, and may we combine them into a public board line, even anonymously?
Cans: price per kg or per can? Households count cans; weigh a sample of local cans to set a factor.

Price basis above the household level: GST-inclusive or exclusive, and do reverse-charge or TDS rules apply when businesses buy metal scrap from unregistered kabadiwalas? This needs a tax adviser before yard prices are shown.
Doorstep vs drop-off: should drop-off pay a published premium, given that doorstep pickup usually needs 25–50 kg or a minimum value (e.g. ₹999 at Kabadiwala Online)?
Should households see named kabadiwalas' prices side by side (open question 3 in pricing.md), or only the city range plus their chosen shop's card?
Is one city-wide floor enough for Bengaluru (open question 2 in pricing.md)? The evidence supports city-wide for the pilot and areas later.
How far do WhatsApp groups and phone calls from the next buyer set daily rates for Bengaluru kabadiwalas and yards? No source opened here documents it; ask in pilot interviews.
At scale, which licensed metal reference (MCX delayed or end-of-day via a vendor, or BigMint), at what yearly cost, and who pays?
Housekeeping: while trying to open the IOSCO benchmark-principles PDF on iosco.org, the Browser pane showed a file-save dialog. The file isn't needed; cancel the dialog if it is still open.

result.headline: Household scrap pickup is proven but thin-margin. Recykal closed its ~0.5-million-download consumer app because each pickup took 45–60 minutes, and the market leader, The Kabadiwala, already runs a partner-kabadiwala marketplace in Bengaluru (Scrapr, 5,000+ kabadiwalas). Luma.Green has to win on reliability, photo estimates, prices shown before booking and a Kannada-first app, not on the marketplace idea itself.

findings.point: Running your own pickup fleet for households loses money. The best-known failure is Recykal's consumer app.
findings.detail: Recykal's Uzed app reached about 0.5 million downloads and around 1,000 orders a day in Hyderabad and Pune. But each order took 45–60 minutes to collect and weigh, and households produced too little material for recyclers. In 2019 Recykal switched to bulk generators (at least 10 kg a day), and revenue grew from ₹1.8 Cr in FY19 to ₹21.2 Cr in FY20. For Luma.Green: sending bookings to existing kabadiwalas avoids the fleet cost that killed Uzed. The pilot still has to show that kabadiwalas find small pickups worth the trip.

findings.point: The market leader already runs Luma.Green's core model, a marketplace of partner kabadiwalas, in Bengaluru.
findings.detail: The Kabadiwala (Bhopal, since 2013) owns vehicles, warehouses and sorting plants (MRFs) in smaller cities. In Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune it uses partner kabadiwalas through its Scrapr app, run by the same company (ASAR Green Kabadi Pvt Ltd). On Scrapr a household enters an address, picks the load size and vehicle, then chooses a partner by distance and price. Scrapr claims 5,000+ kabadiwalas, 11 cities and 25+ Bengaluru neighbourhoods (Koramangala, Indiranagar, Jayanagar). So a marketplace for kabadiwalas is not new on its own. Luma.Green's real differences are the photo estimate, the floor-price table, a Kannada-first app for kabadiwalas with little schooling, and the yard and recycler chain behind the kabadiwala.

findings.point: Funding rounds in consumer scrap pickup are small and the leaders are small companies. The idea is proven, but no one has won the market.
findings.detail: The Kabadiwala has raised $3.33M over 6 rounds (Roots Ventures, ABCOM and others). Tracxn puts its FY25 revenue at ₹10–50 Cr with only 16 staff. It reports 4 lakh+ consumers and 500+ tonnes a month. ScrapUncle raised ₹22 Cr in a pre-Series A round on 28 Jan 2026 (Orios, Acumen). That followed ₹60 lakh for 5% on Shark Tank India season 2 in Feb 2023, a ₹12 Cr valuation, when it had done 22,000 pickups. It now claims 300K+ pickups and 20M kg, with ₹10–50 Cr revenue in FY25 and 63 staff. The only large balance sheet belongs to Attero's MetalMandi (2 lakh+ downloads, 50K+ monthly users, 15,000 tonnes a month by April 2026), which serves dealers rather than households.

findings.point: The top complaints are no-shows and broken promises, not low prices.
findings.detail:
The Kabadiwala's iPhone app has 4.2 stars from 360 ratings. Its reviews describe:
- partners who never arrive
- slow dealer assignment
- a dealer who refused a 14 km trip, while the request stayed stuck and could not be cancelled
- a ₹30 fee on 13 kg when the app promised free pickup above 10 kg (its own terms say 15 kg)

The company's replies send users to a WhatsApp number. EpiCircle (4.7 stars from 105 ratings) has a review about last-minute cancellations with no notice, and Kabadixpress users could not register. When independent dealers do the pickups, their no-shows end up in the platform's reviews.

findings.point: Minimum-load rules differ from player to player and put off households with small amounts.
findings.detail: The Kabadiwala's terms require 15 kg, or 'pickup charges may apply'. Kabadiwala Online (ScrapKabadi) says 'Min pickup ₹999'. ScrapUncle only takes clothes and glass alongside other items and refuses thermocol, wood and ceramics. A 2026 study in three small Indian cities (171 participants) found that small households cannot build up enough recyclables to get regular dealer visits. Luma.Green's drop-off option, with a code to show at the shop, answers this directly and should be shown up front.

findings.point: Published Bengaluru prices for the same material differ by 1.5 to 3 times, so no one yet owns trusted prices.
findings.detail: Newspaper: ₹10/kg at The Kabadiwala, ₹11–13 at ScrapUncle, ₹14–16 at ScrapKabadi. Cardboard: ₹3, ₹7–8 and ₹8–10. Iron: ₹22, ₹20–25 and ₹28–32, while ScrapRates.in (40+ Bengaluru buyers listed) showed ₹39.31/kg on 28 Sep 2026. Copper: ₹500, ₹404–505 and ₹680–720. Sites that only collect leads advertise the highest numbers. Luma.Green's dated floor and fallback tables, plus each kabadiwala's own rate card shown before booking, can become the reference price. The estimate screen should show ranges and say the final rate is set at the door.

findings.point: Households want a reliable pickup time, honest weighing, a fixed price without haggling, and cash or UPI before the collector leaves.
findings.detail: ScrapUncle's founder built the company around missed kabadiwala pickups, inconsistent pricing and no idea where the waste went. On Shark Tank he stressed prices quoted before pickup, safe verified staff and service for apartment residents. ScrapUncle advertises digital weighing and 'instant payment before we leave'. Pune's Scrapdeal, which took no outside funding, reports 80–90% of customers coming back across 500+ housing societies, partly because there is no bargaining. Money is the main reason households sell, but the amounts are small.

findings.point: Booking by WhatsApp or phone is standard, and the leading apps are English-only.
findings.detail:
These players all take bookings or support outside their app:
- The Kabadiwala: WhatsApp Business and phone
- ScrapUncle: WhatsApp
- Crapbin: phone and WhatsApp
- ScrapKabadi: WhatsApp and phone only, with no app
- ScrapQ: a missed-call number

The iPhone app listings of The Kabadiwala and ScrapUncle show English as the only language. Luma.Green's 12 hand-translated languages, led by Kannada, fill a real gap. A way to reach Luma.Green on WhatsApp is probably needed sooner than the 'later' in the current plan.

findings.point: Rewards are mostly referral coupons and environmental-impact stats. The one unusual scheme looks like an investment product.
findings.detail: The Kabadiwala offers referral rewards, coupons, gift cards and 'trees and water saved' stats. EpiCircle lets users convert earnings into gold or silver with '11–15% annual returns', plus green coins and Amazon, Zomato and Domino's coupons. In 2019 Junkart paid by Paytm or let users donate to an NGO. No source links rewards to customers coming back; the retention stories (Scrapdeal, ScrapUncle) are about reliability. Luma.Green's recycle points should stay simple and have no cash value during the pilot, because ADR 0009 keeps money off the platform.

findings.point: No household pickup app advertises a price estimate from photos. The only AI image pricing, MetalMandi, is built for dealers.
findings.detail: The Kabadiwala, ScrapUncle, ScrapQ, EpiCircle, Scrapdeal and Crapbin all price from a material list or by weighing at the door. Kabadiwala Online's enquiry form takes photos, but for a manual quote. Attero's MetalMandi uses AI image detection to identify metal and e-waste scrap and judge its quality, but it serves dealers. Bintix scans packaging with AI behind the scenes to build data for brands. Luma.Green's flow (photo, then materials and a kilogram range, then rupees from its own price tables) stands out for households and makes a strong investor demo.

findings.point: The players that survive move into processing, recycling compliance (EPR) and data. Several consumer-only players have shut down.
findings.detail:
Survivors:
- ScrapUncle is spending its new money on collection infrastructure and a planned in-house e-waste recycling plant.
- Crapbin started in 2018 as a free-pickup online kabadiwala and now calls itself a CPCB/TSPCB-authorised e-waste recycler.
- Kabadiwalla Connect moved from its RecyKle household app (2016) to 'Hyperlokal', a B2B service that sources material through scrap shops (June 2020).
- Bintix earns from consumption data drawn from the packaging of about 41,000 households.

Gone: Junkart (Delhi NCR, Mumbai and Bengaluru in 2019), whose junkart.in domain no longer resolves; Kabadi-Xpress, whose kabadi-xpress.com now redirects to an unrelated site; and Recykal's Uzed. This supports pitching Luma.Green as the whole chain (kabadiwala, yard, recycler, manufacturer, then EPR and carbon) rather than a household app alone.

findings.point: Bengaluru specifics: a city network of dry-waste centres run by waste pickers takes mixed dry waste, brands collect e-waste free, and several app competitors are already here.
findings.detail:
In 2019 Bengaluru had 198 approved Dry Waste Collection Centres (DWCCs), 166 of them working, each handling 0.5–4.5 tonnes a day. Waste pickers ran 33 of them with support from the NGO Hasiru Dala, and about 82% of the dry waste they received was low-value.

EcoFlyp (Aug 2026) lists 10 doorstep e-waste pickups in Bengaluru, mostly free take-back schemes from brands such as Croma, Xiaomi, Samsung, LG, HP and boAt. So e-waste earns households little.

Competitors already in the city:
- The Kabadiwala / Scrapr
- ScrapUncle, whose rate card lists Bengaluru
- Bintix, scanning 58,714 packs a week in Bengaluru
- ScrapKabadi
- ScrapRates.in, with 40+ buyers listed
- Hasiru Dala Innovations, with 370+ business and institutional clients in FY24–25

Luma.Green's money for households lies in paper, metal and plastic. Low-value leftovers could go to DWCCs.

recommendations.feature: Show nearby kabadiwalas side by side on the estimate, with distance and their price for these materials, and tag the best price
recommendations.why: Scrapr already lets households choose a partner by distance and price, and published Bengaluru rates differ by up to 3 times. Showing each verified shop's rate card for the photographed materials (the fallback table where a shop has set none) answers open question 3 in pricing.md. It also makes the 'latest prices' promise visible in the investor demo, using data Luma.Green already stores.

recommendations.feature: Reliability loop: auto-accept, re-offer the booking to the next kabadiwala after a timeout, and a live 'who is coming, when, on the way' screen
recommendations.why: No-shows, slow assignment and stuck requests are the top complaints about The Kabadiwala and EpiCircle. Demoing a booking that moves to the next kabadiwala after the timeout (open question 8), with SMS updates, shows investors that Luma.Green has designed for the problem that hurts the incumbents.

recommendations.feature: Digital receipt after weighing: kg × rate for each material, cash or UPI, estimate against actual, and a kg and CO2e impact line, shareable by link
recommendations.why: Honest weighing and instant payment are what households value, and every leader advertises digital scales and bills. Showing estimate against actual builds trust in the AI and feeds the pilot measures. The impact line sets up the carbon module.

recommendations.feature: A public, search-indexed 'Bengaluru scrap rates today' page built from the dated floor and fallback tables, with history
recommendations.why: City rate pages are how The Kabadiwala, ScrapKabadi and ScrapRates.in attract search traffic. Luma.Green's dated tables already hold this data, so the page costs little. It gives kabadiwalas a reference price and shows investors the planned live-prices module. The numbers should be labelled as indicative.

recommendations.feature: Show each kabadiwala's minimum before booking, offer 'too small for a pickup? drop it off' with the shop code, and never charge a surprise fee
recommendations.why: Minimums differ (15 kg, ₹999, 'only with other items'), and a ₹30 surprise fee led to a public complaint. Showing the minimum at booking and sending small loads to drop-off turns a sore point into a feature. It also uses kabadiwalas without a vehicle, who stay visible for drop-offs.

recommendations.feature: Let each kabadiwala mark every material as 'buys', 'takes free' or 'doesn't take', and show it on the estimate
recommendations.why: The Kabadiwala lists some items at ₹0 instead of refusing them, ScrapUncle refuses thermocol, wood and ceramics, and about 82% of the dry waste reaching Bengaluru's collection centres is low-value. A three-way flag on the existing rate card sets expectations and avoids arguments at the door. Later it lets leftovers be sent to DWCCs.

recommendations.feature: Add a WhatsApp support number (tap to chat) and a 'share to WhatsApp' button on the tracking page now; build the full WhatsApp booking bot later
recommendations.why: Every leader takes bookings or support over WhatsApp or phone, and slow support is a top complaint. A tap-to-chat number and a share button need no WhatsApp API work and cover most of the value until the planned bot is built.

recommendations.feature: Self-serve cancel and reschedule, a two-tap rating after each pickup, and a reliability score for each kabadiwala that affects who gets offered bookings first
recommendations.why: One review describes a request that got stuck and could not be cancelled, and ScrapUncle has added a review for each pickup. Ranking nearby shops partly on their acceptance and completion record from pilot data stops unreliable dealers from damaging the brand.

recommendations.feature: Apartment pickup days: a kabadiwala opens a time slot at a housing complex and residents book into it
recommendations.why: Scrapdeal's 500+ housing societies with 80–90% repeat customers, and Bintix's model of about 41,000 households signed up through their communities, show apartments are the efficient household channel. Grouping pickups raises the kilograms per trip, which was the problem that sank Uzed. Bengaluru's apartment resident associations (RWAs) are an easy way in for the pilot.

recommendations.feature: Make recycle points an impact count (kg recycled, CO2e) with no cash value in the pilot, add referral bonuses later, and never offer gold or 'returns'
recommendations.why: Competitors' rewards are coupons and impact stats, and no source ties them to customers coming back. EpiCircle's '11–15% returns' in gold and silver looks like a financial product. ADR 0009 keeps money off the platform, so points with a cash value would need payments first. This settles open question 6 simply.

recommendations.feature: Send household e-waste to authorised recyclers and brand take-back schemes, with income tied to recycling compliance (EPR) later
recommendations.why: Bengaluru households already have about 10 doorstep e-waste options, most of them free brand take-backs, so e-waste earns them little. Survivors such as Crapbin and ScrapUncle make their money by processing e-waste. Luma.Green should earn through its recycler network rather than compete on the price paid to households.

recommendations.feature: A data product for brands and EPR compliance bodies: anonymised material and packaging data, collected only with consent
recommendations.why: Bintix pays for its household service by selling consumption analysis from the packaging of about 41,000 households. Luma.Green's photos and weighed receipts produce similar data at every step of the chain and could become a second revenue line. This needs explicit consent under India's data-protection law and must keep the 90-day photo deletion rule.

risks: Direct overlap with the leader: The Kabadiwala's Scrapr already runs a partner-kabadiwala marketplace in 25+ Bengaluru neighbourhoods and claims 5,000+ kabadiwalas nationally. Investors who know it will discount a 'marketplace for kabadiwalas' pitch unless Luma.Green leads with the photo estimate, the Kannada-first app for low-literacy kabadiwalas and the full chain.

Thin margins: household loads are small (each Uzed order took 45–60 minutes, and the app closed). If pilot kabadiwalas find pickups unprofitable they will stop accepting them, which is already a stop condition in pilot.md.
Reliability depends on others: independent kabadiwalas' no-shows and refusals become Luma.Green's bad reviews, as The Kabadiwala's App Store reviews show.

Price expectations: some sites advertise newspaper at ₹14–16/kg against ₹10–13 elsewhere. If the estimate or the fallback table is higher than what shops pay at the door, households feel cheated. If the minimum prices are above market, shops refuse bookings.
Rewards and money: points with a cash value, or gold-linked 'returns' like EpiCircle's, raise payment and financial-product questions that ADR 0009 deliberately avoids in the pilot.
Privacy: photos of homes, exact addresses and phone numbers are sensitive. Any data product needs explicit consent and anonymisation under the DPDP Act.

Shutdown history: Junkart, Kabadi-Xpress and Recykal's Uzed are gone. Investors will ask how often households sell and how many come back, which is hard to show in a short pilot because households sell scrap only every few weeks or months.
Data quality: most competitor numbers (users, kg, downloads) are self-reported or Tracxn estimates, and Play Store pages could not be read, so treat the matrix as indicative.
openQuestions: What does Scrapr charge partner kabadiwalas (subscription or commission), and how many of its 5,000+ kabadiwalas are active in Bengaluru? Its pricing page returned 404.
Is ScrapUncle actually operating in Bengaluru? Its rate card lists Bengaluru, but its January 2026 funding news mentions only Delhi NCR.
What minimum load (in kg or ₹) makes a home pickup worth the trip for a Bengaluru kabadiwala, and what share of households reach it? To be measured in the pilot.
When shown both, do households pick the nearest kabadiwala or the one with the best price?
How often does a typical Bengaluru household have enough scrap to sell (monthly, quarterly)? This sets the repeat-use numbers investors will expect.
Can Luma.Green hand low-value materials to waste-picker-run DWCCs or Hasiru Dala, and on what terms?
How many DWCCs operate today under the Greater Bengaluru Authority? The latest figure found (166 working of 198) is from 2019.
Do the Android versions of competitor apps offer Indian languages? Only the iPhone listings were checked, and they show English only.

result.headline: Of 18 recycling platforms reviewed, none connects household bookings, kabadiwala tools and yard-to-recycler trade on one platform that many buyers use. Recykal (₹1,498 crore gross revenue in FY26) only deals with sellers that have verified GST registration, and EPR certificates can only be traded on CPCB's regulated exchange, which charges 4% and requires its operator to earn ₹50 crore a year. So Luma.Green's opening is a traced first mile plus simple yard tools, not bulk trading or EPR credits.

findings.point: EPR certificates can only be traded on an exchange regulated by CPCB, and Luma.Green can neither run nor broker it
findings.detail: CPCB's guidelines for the EPR Electronic Trading & Settlement Platform (EPRETP, issued around January 2025) change who handles what. Certificates are still created on CPCB's EPR portal. Setting prices, trading and payment move to one authorised exchange covering plastic, e-waste, batteries, tyres and used oil. How it works: each week the exchange runs a sealed auction in which buyers and sellers both place orders and all matched trades clear at one price. A market at that fixed price stays open between auctions. CPCB sets a minimum and maximum price every quarter. Buyers pay 100% into an escrow account owned by a bank, and sellers are paid within two days. The fee is 4% (2% from each side) and 30% of it goes to the regulator. Brokers are not allowed. Prices, volumes and past prices must be published as downloads and through an API. To run the exchange a company needs ₹50 crore a year of trading-platform revenue for three years, ₹10 crore average net worth, ten years' experience, and capacity for 50 lakh transactions a year or 1 lakh users. MSTC was recommended as the operator, but as of 26 March 2026 CPCB had not announced a launch date.

findings.point: EPR now covers metal scrap, so yards and recyclers will need proof of where their material came from
findings.detail: MoEFCC brought in EPR for non-ferrous metal scrap on 1 July 2025, in force from 1 April 2026. Companies that make or sell products containing non-ferrous metals must register on CPCB's portal, meet yearly recycling targets, file half-yearly and yearly returns, buy certificates to cover any shortfall, and use a minimum amount of metal recycled in India. The older EPR schemes already split certificates by type. Plastic has three kinds: recycling, end-of-life, and use of recycled content. They come in lots of 1 to 1,000 t and last three years. E-waste certificates are issued per metal: iron, aluminium, copper and gold. Recycling certificates are created by recyclers and processors, who are exactly the buyers Luma.Green's yards sell to.

findings.point: Recykal already runs the bulk-trade features Luma.Green has planned, at scale and in Karnataka
findings.detail: On Recykal.Market's plastic side, sellers are GST-verified and rated. It shows 3,000+ live lots and promises grade testing where the material is loaded. It tracks trucks by GPS with arrival times and finds checked transporters at short notice. Each trade gets a document set (invoice, e-way bill, weight certificate) and a stored bundle of GST records for audits. E-waste lots sell at a fixed price or by one of four auction types: open, sealed, cascaded or reverse. Recykal has sold EPR services to brands since 2019. Gross revenue in FY26 was ₹1,498 crore, up 53% from ₹978 crore, and losses fell to 4% of revenue. It raised a $23M bridge round on 20 June 2026, partly for Europe and the UK. Two gaps: its iOS seller app is in English only (2 ratings) across 16 states including Karnataka, and it deals only with businesses whose GST registration it has checked.

findings.point: Big recyclers are building their own apps to buy straight from dealers and homes
findings.detail: Attero launched MetalMandi in January 2025. Scrap dealers use it to list and sell metal scrap, with prices set by AI and logistics arranged for them. By June 2025 it supplied about 70% of the e-waste Attero bought, and the target was 1,000 t a day by mid-2025. Attero's app for households to hand back old electronics, Selsmart (mid-2024), supplied about 10%. Attero processes 1.44 lakh t of e-waste a year and says 95% of India's e-waste goes through informal hands. Recyclers with their own buying apps will compete for kabadiwala supply, so Luma.Green, which favours no single buyer, should route material to them rather than fight them.

findings.point: Newer Indian B2B marketplaces sell trust: verified buyers, lab tests, escrow and paid tiers
findings.detail: ScrapCart sells factory scrap by live auction, tender or fixed-price listing. It tests metal composition with an XRF analyser, and an outside escrow partner holds the payment until delivery is checked. It claims 200+ verified buyers in Haryana, Gujarat and Maharashtra. Recyclaro (2025; Noida and Dubai) offers listings and requests for quotes (RFQs) from businesses whose identity it has checked. It covers six material families, publishes a daily price index for 12 materials, and says it produces EPR and ESG reports automatically. Pricing: Basic is free (3–5 listings and 2 RFQs a month), Premium ₹8,299 a month, Enterprise ₹24,900 a month, and market data ₹4,199 a month. Both serve registered businesses, not kabadiwalas.

findings.point: PROs and recyclers pay to build traceable supply from informal collectors, mostly by hand
findings.detail: Karo Sambhav is a producer responsibility organisation (PRO): it meets EPR duties on behalf of brands. It barcodes every item, tracks trucks by GPS, and has staff upload photos into an app at pickup. Image recognition then checks an aggregator's bill against what is actually on the truck. It also helps small collectors register for GST and keep bill books (5,000 informal aggregators across 28 states and 3 UTs in 2020). ReCircle runs its own tracking platform, ClimaOne, for plastic credits, working with 3,500+ waste pickers (it calls them Safai Saathis) in 310+ cities and 45 processors; it reports 161,000+ t kept out of landfill. Banyan Nation has mapped and trained thousands of informal collectors and aggregators, and tracks waste from collection to recycling for brands such as Reckitt, Marico and Tata Motors. Luma.Green's pickup and hand-off records would produce this same proof automatically, as part of daily work.

findings.point: The informal first mile avoids GST and digital records, so the app has to be worth using on its own terms
findings.detail: Mongabay (22 May 2026) reports three things. Kabadiwalas prefer cash and avoid GST records so they stay anonymous. EPR rules leave informal collectors out even though they handle most of the waste. And efforts to formalise them are still rare. Kabadiwalla Connect started mapping Chennai's informal network in 2015 and had about 2,000 kabadiwalas on its platform by 2022. It offers apps to plan work and set prices, identity checks, tracking of material through each sale, guaranteed supply for processors, and collection run through local scrap shops. For Luma.Green this means GST must stay optional and cash payments must be recordable.

findings.point: Bengaluru's dry-waste collection centres are organised but still keep their books on paper
findings.detail: Around 2020, Hasiru Dala supported 33 Dry Waste Collection Centres (DWCCs) run by waste-picker entrepreneurs. Its stock system records what comes in from door-to-door collection and drop-offs, and what is sold to recyclers each week. But workers write figures on paper and enter them once a month, so mistakes are only caught afterwards by flagging and reviewing entries. Hasiru Dala Innovations (HDI) now collects seven days a week for 370+ clients that produce waste in bulk. It also supplies fair-trade, fully traceable household plastic to recyclers and brands, with 327 supplier clients. These centres are natural yards for the pilot, and HDI is a local rival for traceable plastic.

findings.point: Yard software abroad is mature; small Indian yards have no simple phone-based equivalent
findings.detail: Scrap Dragon (US) is linked to the weighing scale and takes a photo of the load and the seller's ID automatically at each purchase. It reports to US state metal-theft databases, tracks barcoded stock, runs dispatch with a web app for drivers and connects to accounting software. In India, Recykal's document set and GST records serve the buyer end. Apart from Kabadiwalla Connect's Chennai tools and Hasiru Dala's own system for its centres, no platform reviewed gives small yards a daily stock-and-sales book. A free one would also produce Luma.Green's trace data.

findings.point: Global marketplaces keep listing free and charge for guarantees, data or contracts
findings.detail: Scrapo's plastics marketplace is free on web, iOS and Android. Its paid ScrapoSure service checks the seller, inspects the material, watches the loading, helps with shipping and secures the payment. ScrapMonster publishes scrap prices for the US, Europe, China and India; live prices are for paying subscribers only. It also carries buy and sell offers and a company directory. Circular.co (US, full launch June 2022) adds online contracts, payment handling, logistics and market data for recycled plastics; its partners offered 12 million lb of material a month.

findings.point: Well-funded players have failed by financing trades themselves or brokering on thin margins
findings.detail: Metaloop (Graz) handled the negotiation, transport and payment for trades in secondary metals. It picked material up in about three days and checked it on calibrated scales, by eye, and by chemical (spectral) analysis. A court opened restructuring on 17 June 2026, with about €11.08M owed to 153 creditors and 10 staff affected. This happened even though it had started covering its operating costs in early 2026. When some owners refused to put in more cash, financing every trade became too expensive. Rubicon, a US waste broker, made $4.5M gross profit on $163.1M revenue in Q2 2024. It was delisted from the NYSE in June 2024 and had to sell its fleet software business. The lesson for Luma.Green: never pre-pay for trades and never hold stock of its own.

findings.point: Escrow is normal between businesses, but it needs a regulated partner and has conditions to qualify
findings.detail: CPCB's exchange takes 100% of the buyer's payment into an escrow account owned by a bank. ScrapCart and Scrapo offer escrow or secured payment. Razorpay Route, the payment service named in Luma.Green's ADR 0009, is built for marketplaces that pay many sellers and can hold payouts for a set time. But Razorpay asks businesses to meet turnover minimums and confirm in writing what they will use it for, as RBI requires. Escrow should therefore not be promised for the pilot or the investor demo.

findings.point: No platform reviewed connects household bookings, kabadiwala tools and yard-to-recycler trade
findings.detail: B2B marketplaces deal only with businesses whose GST registration or identity they have checked (Recykal, ScrapCart, Recyclaro). PROs and recyclers reach collectors through their own programmes or buying apps (Karo Sambhav, ReCircle, Banyan Nation, Attero). Specialists in the first mile each work in one city (Kabadiwalla Connect in Chennai, Hasiru Dala in Bengaluru). The global players are trading or data sites built for registered companies. Luma.Green's single record from household to manufacturer, in 12 languages and with GST optional, fills the space none of them cover.

recommendations.feature: Lot history with a shareable origin sheet
recommendations.why: Recykal, Karo Sambhav, ReCircle, Banyan Nation and ScrapCart all sell traceability, but each starts after the first mile. Show one lot (say 320 kg of newspaper) with every hand-off: the pickups it came from (area only), weights, photos, prices and times. Then offer a QR code or PDF sheet the yard can pass on to its buyer. It reads the stock-movement records already planned, and it is the clearest investor demo of what makes Luma.Green different. Call it an origin record, never an EPR certificate.

recommendations.feature: Two-way stock board: kabadiwalas post what they have, yards post what they want; accept or make one counter-offer
recommendations.why: Listings with negotiation are the norm (Recykal's moderated deals, Recyclaro's requests for quotes). Auctions (Recykal e-waste, ScrapCart, CPCB's exchange) suit big industrial lots, not a shop's 300 kg of paper. Letting both sides post answers the open question of who starts a trade without choosing one. Minimum quantities and search distance go in tables the admin can edit.

recommendations.feature: Verified badge on every business card, showing how long its consent document is valid
recommendations.why: Every B2B rival leads with verification: Recykal checks GST for every seller, Recyclaro checks identity, ScrapCart verifies its buyers. Luma.Green already checks every business by hand. Showing 'verified on <date>, pollution-board consent valid until <date>' in listings costs little and puts that trust on screen.

recommendations.feature: Bengaluru price board built from recorded trades
recommendations.why: ScrapMonster, Recyclaro (₹4,199 a month) and MetalMandi sell quotes, price indexes or AI prices. Luma.Green can show what was actually paid at each hand-off, for example the typical (median) ₹/kg for each material over the last 7 days, from household to kabadiwala and from kabadiwala to yard, next to the admin minimum. It comes from data the pilot records anyway (sample data can fill it for the demo) and grows into the planned live-prices module.

recommendations.feature: Hand-over check on both sides: weight, a photo of each material, and a dispute button
recommendations.why: Weight and grade checks are expected everywhere (Recykal grade testing, ScrapCart composition tests, Metaloop calibrated scales). When a kabadiwala hands a load to a yard, both sides confirm the weight (shop scale against yard weighbridge) and a photo of each material. A difference bigger than an allowance the admin sets (for example 2%) opens a dispute for the admin. The confirmed figures feed the lot history.

recommendations.feature: Free yard book: stock in and out, sorting, sales, photo of the weighbridge slip
recommendations.why: Yard software like Scrap Dragon has no simple Indian-language equivalent that works on a phone, and Hasiru Dala's system for its centres still starts on paper with monthly entry. A daily book using the same stock tables as the kabadiwala app gives yards a reason to open Luma.Green every day and produces trace data.

recommendations.feature: Trade documents generated from the record
recommendations.why: Recykal wins recyclers with a document set per trade (invoice, e-way bill, weight certificate) and stored GST records. Luma.Green can produce one PDF per trade with a delivery challan or draft invoice, weight slip and photos, add the GST number when there is one, and pre-fill the e-way bill fields for loads that need one, without filing anything.

recommendations.feature: Record proof of payment now; add escrow later through a licensed partner
recommendations.why: Escrow is standard between businesses (CPCB's bank escrow, ScrapCart, ScrapoSure), but Razorpay Route has turnover and RBI conditions. Metaloop failed once financing trades became too costly. In the pilot, record the UPI reference or a photo of the cash receipt for each trade and mark advance payments. Never pre-pay for trades, hold stock or hold anyone's money. Add Route or a bank escrow when trade volume justifies it.

recommendations.feature: Bring Bengaluru's dry-waste collection centres on as yards
recommendations.why: The centres run by waste pickers (33 supported by Hasiru Dala) already sort dry waste and sell to recyclers, and Hasiru Dala Innovations sells traceable plastic. Partnering gives the pilot real yard volume and turns a likely rival into a supplier on the platform. It needs only a 'collection centre' flag on the existing yard type, not a new role.

recommendations.feature: EPR evidence export for registered recyclers and PROs
recommendations.why: Recyclers and processors create the certificates and trade them on CPCB's exchange, which does not allow brokers and requires its operator to earn ₹50 crore a year. Luma.Green's part is the evidence. It can export each lot's origin area, weights, photos, GPS and dates, sorted into CPCB's categories (plastic Cat I–III; e-waste iron, aluminium, copper, gold; non-ferrous metals from April 2026). Once the exchange is live, it can also read the exchange's published prices through its API.

recommendations.feature: Free for the first mile; paid plans for yards, recyclers and manufacturers
recommendations.why: Price points to compare: Recyclaro charges ₹8,299–24,900 a month, ScrapMonster charges for live prices, Scrapo charges for its guarantee service, and CPCB's exchange takes 4% per trade. Rubicon's thin broker margin ($4.5M gross profit on $163.1M in one quarter) shows a cut of each trade may not be enough to fund the business. Charge buyers for exports, trade documents, analytics and API access, and never take a share of the kabadiwala's cash.

Brokers earn thin margins (Rubicon: $4.5M gross profit on $163.1M revenue in Q2 2024), so a cut of each trade alone may not pay for running the platform.

What do Recykal and MetalMandi charge small aggregators, and what are their minimum lot sizes and payment terms? None of this is published.
Which Bengaluru materials (paper, PET, metals) move from kabadiwalas to yards in enough volume to show real matches in the investor demo?
Can a young company like Luma.Green meet Razorpay Route's turnover minimums, or will escrow need a bank partner?
Does helping businesses trade make Luma.Green a GST 'e-commerce operator' that must collect tax on each sale? (open question 12 in docs/product/open-questions.md)
