result.headline: India's recycling runs on an informal first mile: 1.5–4 million waste pickers, plus kabadiwalas and two or three tiers of dealers, move 60–70% of urban recyclables, and value leaks at every hop. This week a Bengaluru household gets ₹500–590/kg for copper that trades at ₹1,394–1,454/kg, about 35–42% of the wholesale price.

findings.point: The material that reaches Indian mills is worth at least ₹1.8–2.1 lakh crore (about $20–24B) a year, and ferrous scrap is 80–85% of it. Every stream is growing.
findings.detail:
This is our own bottom-up estimate: cited volumes multiplied by current factory-gate prices.
- Ferrous scrap: 41 Mt used in FY2024-25 at ₹36.5–41.5/kg (BigMint, 23 Sep 2026) comes to ₹1.50–1.70 lakh crore.
- Recovered paper: about 17 Mt (roughly 75% of the 23 Mt of paper made in 2024-25) at ₹14–18/kg delivered to mills comes to ₹0.24–0.31 lakh crore.
- Plastics: 2.5 Mt of EPR-certified processing (2022-23) at ₹10–44/kg comes to ₹0.03–0.11 lakh crore.

Copper, aluminium, brass, lead, glass, e-waste, textiles and tyres are not included, so treat the total as a floor. The dollar figure assumes ₹88 to the dollar.

Industry framing:
- MRAI (citing an Avendus report) puts the recycling market at about $20B by 2030, with 2.5 million jobs and a network of 25,000 MSMEs (Nov 2025).
- The Ministry of Textiles projects textile recycling alone at $3.5B by 2030 (Feb 2026).

Growth:
- Domestic steel scrap generation is expected to grow 6–8% a year to 2050.
- Official e-waste rose 11% from FY2023-24 to FY2024-25. NITI Aayog projects 17% a year.
- Li-ion batteries reaching end of life go from 19 kt (2023) to 233 kt by 2035.
- Urban municipal waste is 1,66,096 t/day, 80.17% of it processed (MoHUA, 1 Dec 2025).

findings.point: Informal workers run the first mile: 60–70% of urban recyclables, about 62–75% of e-waste and 70% of retired batteries.
findings.detail:
- **Waste pickers:** Down To Earth (15 May 2026, citing the ILO and Chintan) counts 1.5–4 million informal waste pickers. They handle 60–70% of urban recyclables and about 70% of plastic recycling. They earn ₹200–400 on a good day, typically under ₹10,000 a month.
- **E-waste:** NITI Aayog (Jan 2026) says about 62% is handled informally. The Chatter (Apr 2026) says the formal share rose from about 1% to about 25% after the 2022 EPR rules.
- **Batteries:** in 2020, 70% of retired batteries were collected by informal aggregators, 20% by manufacturers and 10% by formal handlers (WRI India, Jul 2024).

What this means for Luma.Green: the supply side is people who are paid in cash, often undocumented and on a first smartphone. The onboarding and household flows must work for them.

findings.point: Four to six hand-offs sit between a household and a factory. Luma.Green's roles assume one yard between kabadiwala and recycler.
findings.detail:
- **Plastics:** CSE maps the unorganised chain as household or waste picker → kabadiwala → small dealer → medium dealer → large dealer → recycler, then a converter or manufacturer.
- **Textiles:** brokers appear at several steps: collector → local aggregator → trader → shredder → open-end spinning mill (Fashion for Good, 2022). South India's cutting waste goes to the Tirupur–Coimbatore–Erode belt. Panipat takes in 3,500–5,250 t/day (Ministry of Textiles, 2026).
- **Ferrous scrap:** it moves through area aggregators to furnace hubs such as Mandi Gobindgarh, the market behind BigMint's index.

Each hop adds sorting, baling, freight, credit and a margin.

What this means for the data model: yards must be able to buy from other yards, with a size or tier attribute, rather than a new role for each dealer tier.

findings.point: Hidden prices are the biggest leak. Bengaluru households get about 35–42% of the wholesale price for copper and about 23% for PET bottles.
findings.detail:
Prices at the household's door in Bengaluru (The Kabadiwala; scraprates.in, 28 Sep 2026):
- copper ₹500–588/kg
- brass ₹400–439/kg
- aluminium ₹150–154/kg
- iron ₹22–39/kg
- PET ₹10/kg
- newspaper ₹10–14/kg
- cardboard ₹3–8/kg

Factory or wholesale prices:
- copper ₹1,394/kg on MCX (28 Sep 2026); copper armature ₹1,454/kg in Delhi
- brass ₹950–990/kg in Delhi
- aluminium ₹293–365/kg in Delhi
- ferrous index ₹41.5/kg; HMS 80:20 ₹36.5/kg in Mumbai (23 Sep 2026)
- PET bottle scrap ₹44/kg in Bengaluru (Sep 2026)
- baled cardboard (OCC) ₹14–18/kg delivered to mills (Apr 2026)

Share of the factory price the household gets:
- copper about 35–42%
- brass about 40–46%
- aluminium about 50%
- PET about 23%
- cardboard about 20–55%
- iron about 55–100% (the narrowest gap)

Sorting, cleaning, grade, freight and credit explain part of each gap. The widest gaps, though, are in metals priced off an exchange, where door rates lag the market. That points to missing information more than to cost.

findings.point: Rigged scales have been found in Bengaluru scrap shops.
findings.detail:
- **March 2023, Kamakshipalya:** a resident selling about 40 kg of newspapers at an old-paper shop saw the reading being adjusted with a remote. Police then arrested 17 shopkeepers from scrap shops, ration shops and meat stalls. Their scales had circuit-board chips fitted by two former contract technicians of the Legal Metrology department (Deccan Herald, 19 Mar 2023).
- **Official enforcement:** Karnataka's Legal Metrology department booked 5,375 cases in Bengaluru Urban in the 17 months to Aug 2024, with ₹1.79 crore in fines. It takes complaints on emapan.karnataka.gov.in (NewsKarnataka, Nov 2024).

What this means for Luma.Green: a receipt that both sides confirm is a trust feature for households, not an extra.

findings.point: Moisture and contamination take 20–50% of the value, mostly off the record.
findings.detail:
- **Cardboard:** wet cardboard loses 30–50% of its value and may be rejected (BIN, Apr 2026).
- **Bengaluru dry waste:** operators of the city's dry waste collection centres (DWCCs) say only about 30% of incoming dry waste is good enough to earn from. In the rains, pickers have to dry material before they can sell it (Citizen Matters, Sep 2025).
- **Textiles:** garment cutting waste sold mixed carries up to 20% contamination and fetches ₹6–35/kg. Sorted white cuttings fetch ₹50–60/kg (Fashion for Good, 2022).

What this means for Luma.Green: every business-to-business hand-off needs a quality grade and an explicit deduction line: gross weight, deduction, reason and net weight.

findings.point: Cash, credit and the 18% GST keep trade informal. Since October 2024 the tax burden on metal scrap has shifted to yards.
findings.detail:
- **Cash:** collectors on the ground buy in cash and avoid digital payments (Karo Sambhav, quoted by Mongabay, 22 May 2026).
- **Tax:** MRAI says the 18% GST on recycled materials is unaffordable for small operators, which keeps them outside GST (Nov 2025). WRI blames the same 18% on retired batteries for diverting them to informal recyclers. The Chatter notes informal e-waste buyers outbid formal ones because they carry no GST overhead.
- **Metal scrap rules:** since 10 Oct 2024, a registered buyer of metal scrap (tariff chapters 72–81) from an unregistered seller pays the GST itself under reverse charge (Notification 06/2024-CT(R)). Business-to-business supplies also carry 2% GST TDS.

What this means for Luma.Green: record payments and amounts owed without moving money, and keep the GST number optional.

findings.point: Price swings are large enough to stop collection altogether.
findings.detail:
- **Paper, 2023:** kraft waste paper fell to ₹11,000–13,500/t (₹11–14/kg) in mid-2023. Domestic collection of recovered paper dropped 50–55% and many collectors quit (IRPTA, via The Pulp and Paper Times, Jun 2023).
- **Steel scrap, Sep 2026:** a north Indian mill owner said mills had cut scrap buying by 50–60% amid oversupply, and the ferrous index slipped to ₹41,500/t (BigMint, 23 Sep 2026).
- **Bengaluru:** dry waste collection centres turn pickers away when rates fall (Citizen Matters, Sep 2025).

What this means for Luma.Green: an admin minimum price that is right today can be above the market within weeks.

findings.point: India is short of domestic scrap and fibre. The bottleneck is collection, not demand, which is why mills should pay for sorted, traceable supply.
findings.detail:
- **Paper:** India made about 23 Mt in 2024-25, around 75% of it from recovered fibre. Yet domestic recovery is only about 30%, and about 7 Mt of recovered paper is imported every year (Waste & Recycling Magazine citing the paper makers' association IPMA, 9 Jan 2026).
- **Steel:** 41 Mt of ferrous scrap was used in FY2024-25, about a quarter of it imported. Scrap is only about 23% of steel feed, against a 2047 goal of 50%. By March 2025, 48 countries restricted scrap exports (Dialogue Earth, 7 May 2026).

This gives Luma.Green's pitch to recyclers and manufacturers a structural basis.

findings.point: Plastics, e-waste, batteries and tyres fall under producer-responsibility (EPR) rules, which add a second price for proof of recycling on top of the material.
findings.detail:
- **Plastics:** officially 4.13 Mt was generated in 2020-21. In 2022-23, EPR obligations were about 3 Mt and processors issued 2.5 Mt of certificates (PIB, 27 Jul 2023).
- **E-waste:** 12.54 lakh t (FY2023-24), 13.98 lakh t (FY2024-25) and 14.14 lakh t (FY2025-26) were generated, with 9.79 lakh t recycled in FY2025-26 (PIB; Lok Sabha, 9 Mar 2026). EPR certificates trade at ₹10–50/kg, with a ₹22/kg floor set in March 2024 that large manufacturers are challenging in the Delhi High Court (The Chatter, Apr 2026).
- **Tyres:** EPR since 2022, with a 100% target from 2024-25. India imported 13.72 lakh t of waste rubber in FY2024-25. Only 296 of 736 tyre-oil (pyrolysis) plants are registered. Imported tyres cost ₹2–5/kg against ₹20–25/kg for domestic ones, because India has no collection centres for used tyres (The Reporters' Collective, Feb 2026).

What this means for Luma.Green: a documented chain from household to recycler is worth money to recyclers and brands, and hazardous streams must go only to authorised buyers.

findings.point: Official figures undercount, so Luma.Green's transaction records are themselves an asset.
findings.detail:
- **E-waste:** the Central Pollution Control Board estimates 1.40 Mt for FY2024-25, from sales data and product lifetimes. NITI Aayog's January 2026 report says 6.19 Mt in 2024, with only about 10% recycled formally.
- **Plastics:** a Nature study (Oct 2024) estimates India emits 9.3 Mt a year of plastic pollution, over twice the official 4.1 Mt of plastic waste. It notes official data leave out rural areas, open burning and informal recycling.

Nobody holds data on weight, material, price, place and date at each hand-off. Luma.Green's receipts would.

findings.point: Bengaluru already has infrastructure run by waste pickers, and it is fraying.
findings.detail:
- **Volumes:** Bengaluru produces 5,000–6,000 t/day of solid waste, run by Bengaluru Solid Waste Management Ltd (Citizen Matters, Apr 2026). That is about 3% of India's urban total. Waste pickers process about 800 t/day of recyclables (Hasiru Dala, via The South First, Mar 2025) and save the city about ₹84 crore a year (Down To Earth, May 2026).
- **Recognition:** the city corporation (BBMP) issued waste-picker ID cards from 2011. It set up 198 dry waste collection centres (DWCCs), one per ward, in 2012-13.
- **Decline:** by September 2025, 141 centres remained and 119 were operating across 127 wards. Hasiru Dala supports 35 of them. The ID cards have expired and the 2020 agreements with the city have lapsed (Citizen Matters, Sep 2025).
- **Earnings:** a good month at one centre earns about ₹1.5 lakh, shared among 20–25 workers. City waste bye-laws (2020) let pickers keep income from selling dry waste.
- **Plastics:** Karnataka generated 3.68 lakh t of plastic waste in 2020-21 (PIB).

findings.point: For bulky, low-value streams such as glass, old clothes and packaging film, households get almost nothing.
findings.detail:
- **Glass:** about 3 Mt of waste a year, 35–45% recycled (Saahas Zero Waste). Households in Delhi NCR get ₹1–2/kg (Recycle Baba). Crushed white glass (cullet) sells at ₹5–12/kg (IndiaMART listings).
- **Textiles:** 7.07 Mt a year (2.97 Mt from factories before sale, 4.10 Mt from households), plus 0.6 Mt imported. 97% of factory waste is recycled, but about 1.9 Mt of household textiles is landfilled or burned (Ministry of Textiles, Feb 2026). Households get about ₹2/kg for old clothes. Bengaluru is a garment-making hub, and its cutting waste goes to the Tirupur belt.
- **Packaging:** The Kabadiwala lists milk covers and packaging film at ₹0/kg.

What this means for Luma.Green: the AI estimate should say "no cash value, free take-away" for these items instead of showing ₹0. Recycle points can reward them.

recommendations.feature: Reference price shown beside the kabadiwala's price. Add a dated `referencePrices` table (city or market, material, paise per kg, source, effectiveFrom) that the admin fills weekly from MCX, BigMint and mill notices. It follows the same pattern as `priceFloors` and `fallbackRates`.
recommendations.why: In Bengaluru, door prices for copper, brass and aluminium are 35–50% of wholesale, and PET is about 23%. Showing the reference price in the kabadiwala rate card and in the admin and investor view makes the promise to "see the latest prices" visible straight away. Decide in the pilot whether households see it too.

recommendations.feature: Material catalogue kept as admin-editable data, with a unit (kg or piece), a value class (cash, points only, not accepted), a hazardous flag and an authorised-buyer-only flag. Rate cards also accept a price per piece.
recommendations.why: Names and grades change at every hop. Appliances are bought per piece at the door (laptop ₹250, fridge ₹350–550, air conditioner ₹2,500–3,000), which a paise-per-kg rate card cannot express. Milk covers and film are worth ₹0. Batteries, e-waste and tyres legally need authorised buyers.

recommendations.feature: Investor dashboard showing the Bengaluru chain in numbers: kg by material, rupees paid to households, the household's share of the factory price, hand-offs recorded and weight disputes. Add a panel of sourced national figures.
recommendations.why: Investors need the size of the market and the leak on one screen. Sourced figures include 41 Mt of ferrous scrap, 23 Mt of paper at 75% recycled fibre, 14.1 lakh t of e-waste, 7.07 Mt of textiles, 1.5–4 million waste pickers and at least ₹1.8–2.1 lakh crore of annual flow. Seeded demo data is enough for the prototype.

recommendations.feature: Weighing receipt that both sides confirm. On `pickupReceipts`, add an optional photo of the scale display, a household confirm tap, and an automatic flag when the weighed kg is far below the AI estimate. Show the kabadiwala scale's Legal Metrology stamp date, checked during onboarding.
recommendations.why: Bengaluru scrap shops have been caught with scales fitted with remote-controlled chips (2023). Bengaluru Urban saw 5,375 Legal Metrology cases in 17 months. Being cheated on weight is the household's first fear.

recommendations.feature: Gross, deduction and net on every business-to-business hand-off: gross grams, deduction %, reason (moisture, contamination, tare), net grams and a quality grade on kabadiwala-to-yard trades.
recommendations.why: Wet cardboard loses 30–50% of its value. Only about 30% of what reaches Bengaluru's dry waste collection centres is good enough to earn from, and textile cutting waste carries up to 20% contamination. Deductions are where disputes happen, and today none of them are written down.

recommendations.feature: A simple khata (credit ledger) on trades: amount due, due date, part payments and the cash or UPI reference. No money moves on the platform, which keeps ADR 0009 intact.
recommendations.why: Trade in this chain runs on cash and credit. Since October 2024, reverse-charge GST on metal scrap bought from unregistered sellers pushes working-capital strain onto yards. Recording who owes whom is the first step towards escrow later.

recommendations.feature: Onboard dry waste collection centres (DWCCs) and waste-picker cooperatives as sellers: a DWCC flag on kabadiwala-type organisations, recruited with Hasiru Dala.
recommendations.why: About 800 t/day of Bengaluru's recyclables already pass through waste pickers, and 119 centres are operating. They need buyers and fair prices: their ID cards have expired and their agreements with the city have lapsed. Partnering with them brings immediate supply to yards and avoids political pushback.

recommendations.feature: Guardrails on the minimum price. Each floor can be set as a percentage of the reference price, with an admin override and a suspend switch per material. Rows stay dated.
recommendations.why: The 2023 waste-paper crash halved collection, and in September 2026 mills cut scrap buying by 50–60%. A fixed floor can end up above the market and stop trade within weeks.

recommendations.feature: Only authorised buyers for hazardous streams. A yard or recycler must upload its state pollution board authorisation or EPR registration before it can buy lead-acid batteries, e-waste or tyres.
recommendations.why: Informal smelters and unregistered tyre-oil plants (440 of 736) outbid formal recyclers. Connecting hazardous waste to unauthorised buyers is a legal and reputational risk for the platform.

recommendations.feature: Chain-of-custody export for EPR and buyers: lot IDs linking pickup receipts, stock and trades with weights and dates, exported as CSV or PDF.
recommendations.why: Recyclers need documented feedstock to claim EPR certificates, which trade at ₹10–50/kg for e-waste; plastics processors issued 2.5 Mt of certificates in 2022-23. Mills short of domestic scrap and fibre will pay for traceable supply.

recommendations.feature: Metal-scrap GST helper: tag tariff chapters 72–81, record each seller's GST status, show the buyer when reverse charge or 2% TDS applies, and produce a purchase voucher. Informational only, not tax advice.
recommendations.why: From 10 October 2024, the buyer pays the GST on metal scrap bought from unregistered kabadiwalas, and business-to-business supplies carry 2% TDS. Yards will need this before they move volume onto the platform.

recommendations.feature: A monthly Luma.Green first-mile scrap index per city: median household price, kabadiwala-to-yard price and the spread for each material, built from the platform's receipts.
recommendations.why: Official volumes are disputed, and metals already have BigMint and MCX indices. No first-mile price series exists. Publishing one is how the platform starts to set the industry's norms.

How to read the table:
- **Household end** is what a kabadiwala pays at the door in Bengaluru (The Kabadiwala, an undated page; scraprates.in, 28 Sep 2026), unless the row says Delhi NCR.
- **Factory end** is the price for a traded grade at a mill, smelter or recycler.
- **Household share** is the door price divided by the factory price, as a rough guide. Sorting, cleaning, grade, freight and credit explain part of every gap.
- **Volumes** for e-waste and plastics are disputed; see the findings.
- **Before use:** re-check the door prices with 10–20 Bengaluru shops before they seed the fallback table.
risks: Showing factory prices to households may turn kabadiwalas against the platform. Their margin pays for sorting, transport, rent, credit and losses. Show the reference price to kabadiwalas and investors first, and test how households react in the pilot.

Some price sources limit redistribution (MCX, BigMint, ScrapMonster). Others are unverified aggregators (scraprates.in, rate-list sites) or undated pages (The Kabadiwala). Label every reference price with its source and date, call it indicative, and never promise it.

Market figures conflict by large factors: e-waste is 1.4 Mt by the pollution board and 6.19 Mt by NITI Aayog; plastics are 4.1 Mt officially against 9.3 Mt of pollution. The ₹1.8–2.1 lakh crore flow is our own estimate. Every investor slide must cite and define its number.

Recording informal cash trades may raise GST questions for users (18% GST, reverse charge on metal scrap) and put them off. Keep the GST number optional and get tax advice before adding any invoice or voucher feature.
Batteries, e-waste and tyres must go to authorised recyclers under the 2022 rules. The platform could be liable if it matches them with unauthorised buyers.
Admin minimum prices can freeze trade in a price crash. That happened in the 2023 waste-paper slump and the steel-scrap buying cuts of September 2026.

Waste-picker politics in Bengaluru are sensitive: the city's agreements with waste pickers have lapsed, their ID cards have expired and the waste company is under Lokayukta scrutiny. A platform seen as displacing waste pickers could meet resistance; partnering with Hasiru Dala-type groups lowers the risk.
Weights recorded in the app are not certified weights under Legal Metrology law. The shop's stamped scale stays the legal instrument, so never market receipts as certified weights.
openQuestions: How many kabadiwalas operate in Bengaluru, and what share of household dry waste reaches them rather than the city's waste company or the dry waste collection centres? No census was found.
What margin does a Bengaluru kabadiwala actually keep per material after rent, transport, credit and losses? Interview 10–20 shops before households see reference prices.
What are the usual payment terms from yard to kabadiwala in Bengaluru (cash at pickup, or 7–30 days' credit), and what are the minimum lot sizes per material?
Which reference-price sources can be used legally and cheaply: MCX, a BigMint subscription, mill price notices?
For investors, should we quote the pollution board's 1.4 Mt of e-waste or NITI Aayog's 6.19 Mt? Or both, with how each is measured?
Has the replacement for the Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 come into force, and does it require kabadiwalas or aggregators to register? This was not verified here.
Should batteries, e-waste and tyres be left out of the Bengaluru pilot entirely until the authorised-buyer check exists?
Can recycle points reward zero-value items (glass, film, old clothes) without distorting the cash prices for other materials?

result.headline: India's compliance carbon market (CCTS) is expected to see its first trades around October 2026, but none of its 8 approved offset methodologies credits recycling. That leaves voluntary plastic credits as Luma's realistic credit route: 1 credit = 1 tonne of plastic, selling for $106–$804 on PCX, against a 2024 voluntary carbon average of $6.34/tCO2e. Every route needs per-lot dry weights from calibrated scales, invoices and receiver GRNs, and an unbroken chain of custody recorded from day one.

findings.point: India's compliance carbon market exists on paper but has not traded yet. First CCC trades are expected around October 2026.
findings.detail: The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme was notified on 28 Jun 2023 (S.O. 2825(E)) and amended in Dec 2023 (S.O. 5369(E)) to add an offset mechanism. The roles: BEE is administrator, Grid Controller of India (Grid-India) runs the registry, and CERC regulates trading. 1 CCC = 1 tCO2e. CERC's CCC Regulations were notified 27 Feb 2026 (Gazette 3 Mar 2026). Their rules: trading only on power exchanges, in monthly sessions; a floor and forbearance price band that CERC approves on BEE's proposal; sale bids capped at registry holdings; and a six-month bar after more than 3 defaults in a quarter. Banking is unlimited and borrowing is not allowed. An obligated entity that falls short pays twice the average CCC price, imposed by CPCB. No CCC price has been discovered yet. Carbon Pulse reports first compliance trades expected in Oct 2026, and CLII says the registry was not fully operational as of Nov 2025.

findings.point: The obligated sectors include several of Luma's future buyers: pulp & paper, aluminium (including secondary aluminium), textiles and petrochemicals. Traceable scrap therefore has indirect compliance value.
findings.detail: Final GHG emission-intensity targets were notified in two rounds. On 8 Oct 2025: aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali and pulp & paper (282 plants). On 16 Jan 2026: refineries, petrochemicals, textiles and secondary aluminium. Iron & steel and fertiliser were still pending at ICAP's update. About 740 entities across nine sectors are expected. Compliance years are FY2025-26 and FY2026-27 against a FY2023-24 baseline, with the reduction back-loaded 40%/60%. Pulp & paper cuts go up to 15% over two years. Offsets cannot be used for compliance. The scheme scores each plant's own gate-to-gate intensity, not its scrap supplier. Even so, more recovered fibre, secondary aluminium or recycled PET lowers a buyer's intensity. Documented, lot-level recycled input is therefore a selling point for Luma's yards and recyclers.

findings.point: None of the 8 approved Indian offset methodologies credits recycling or material recovery. The only waste-sector ones deal with landfill methane.
findings.detail: Under the offset mechanism, any non-obligated entity can register a project that started on or after 1 Jan 2025, in one of ten approved sectors. Phase I covers energy, industries, agriculture, waste handling and disposal, forestry and transport. Phase II adds fugitive emissions, construction, solvent use and CCUS. IETA lists the 8 methodologies approved in March 2025: grid renewable power, electrolytic hydrogen, industrial energy efficiency and fuel switching, hydrogen from biogas methane, landfill methane recovery, flaring or use of landfill gas, manure methane at households and small farms, and mangrove afforestation. Other summaries name RE with storage, offshore wind and compressed biogas instead. Either way, no methodology covers material recovery. A project may not be registered with another carbon market at the same time; India's Green Credit Programme is the only exception. I found no Karnataka-specific carbon rule. Karnataka matters through KSPCB consents and Bengaluru's informal collection chain.

findings.point: India does not currently authorise recycling credits for international transfer. Its Article 6.4 list (7 Jun 2024) has 14 activities, and none is recycling.
findings.detail: The MoEFCC office memorandum lists: renewable energy with storage, solar thermal, offshore wind, green hydrogen, compressed biogas, fuel-cell mobility, high-end energy efficiency, sustainable aviation fuel, best available technology in hard-to-abate sectors, ocean energy, HVDC with renewables, clean cooking (government or PPP only), green ammonia and CCUS. The list holds for an initial 3 years. According to IETA, CCCs from activities on India's Article 6.2 list can seek authorisation with a corresponding adjustment, and non-authorised credits may still be sold for voluntary use. Any recycling credit from India will therefore be a non-authorised voluntary credit for now. That works for corporate contribution claims but is weaker for buyers who need corresponding adjustments.

findings.point: Voluntary carbon methodologies for recycling exist but are narrow: Verra VMR0007 covers plastics, container glass, aluminium and steel; Gold Standard 448 covers metals, alloys and minerals. Neither covers paper.
findings.detail: VMR0007 v1.0 has been active since 4 Sep 2023. It is used together with CDM AMS-III.AJ and adds a discount factor for the uncertain displacement of virgin material. It covers HDPE, LDPE, PET, PVC, PP, container glass cullet, aluminium and steel. AMS-III.AJ on its own closed to new VCS projects on 4 Sep 2023. Gold Standard 448 v1.0 (2 May 2025, developed by South Pole) credits metals, alloys and minerals recovered from municipal solid waste. Its main terms: micro projects ≤10,000 tCO2e/yr and small ≤60,000; crediting for up to 15 years, starting at most 2 years before design certification; crediting stops once a legal mandate takes effect; a default baseline adjustment of 99% that falls 1 point a year; and only recovery that is above legal mandates and not common practice. It monitors weighed quantities cross-checked with invoices, electricity (meter or bills), fuel, and transport emissions per route. It also needs composition and quality evidence to set a substitution factor.

findings.point: Plastic credits, priced per tonne of material, are the most relevant voluntary instrument (Verra WCC/WRC, PCX, Plastic Bank), but the market is small.
findings.detail: Verra's Plastic Program issues Waste Collection Credits and Waste Recycling Credits. Each equals 1 tonne collected or recycled above the baseline, under PWRM0001 v1.1 (30 Jun 2022) and PWRM0002 v1.1. Verra's page cites 40+ projects, 40,000+ credits and 25+ countries, including Project Hara Kal in Kerala; baselines are reset every 7 years. PCX's Plastic Pollution Reduction Standard v8 (5 Jun 2024) made third-party VVBs mandatory for both registration and issuance, dropped landfill activities, and paused 'net zero plastic' claims. PCX reported 29 projects in 7 markets and 87,842 t diverted as of 31 Mar 2024; its credits can be transferred once, then are retired. Plastic Bank defines a credit per traceable kilogram. It pays collectors the cash market rate plus a digital bonus and tiered social benefits, issues one claim ID per purchaser, and runs annual third-party audits.

findings.point: On prices, plastic credits pay far more per tonne of plastic than carbon credits do.
findings.detail: Ecosystem Marketplace (SOVCM 2025) reports that the 2024 voluntary carbon market traded 84.4 MtCO2e for $535.1M, an average of $6.34/tCO2e (2023: $6.71). By category: waste disposal $6.72 on 4.8 Mt (volume +226%, driven by landfill gas), renewable energy $2.67, energy efficiency and fuel switching $3.05, household devices $7.30. A retail listing for a PET-recycling carbon credit (Greentech, Romania, Gold Standard) asks $29/tCO2e. PCX plastic credits list at $106–$804 per tonne of plastic, about ₹9–70/kg at an assumed ₹87/US$. At $6.72/tCO2e, a material would have to avoid about 15.8 tCO2e per tonne just to match the lowest plastic-credit price. For plastics the plastic credit therefore dominates; carbon credits matter mostly for metals. CCC prices under CCTS have not been discovered yet.

findings.point: What verifiers check under Verra's plastic methodologies: dispatch-level dry weights on calibrated scales, cross-checked against invoices, payment receipts and the receiver's goods receipt note (GRN).
findings.detail: PWRM0001 Table 3: plastic sent to each destination is weighed dry at the collection facility before dispatch, at the end destination, or both. It is recorded every time material leaves and cross-checked with invoices, payment receipts and GRNs. Weighbridges are calibrated to the manufacturer's specification or at least every 3 years. Section 9.3 requires written procedures for each measurement task, electronic logging, version control, trained staff and data-integrity checks, with archives kept for at least 2 years after the crediting period. PWRM0002 adds: sorted output by material type for each batch (at least daily); a per-batch list of recycling inputs, aggregated monthly; recycled output weighed after the final stage, after drying if washed, and cross-checked with sales receipts; and removal of hazardous material. PCX chain-of-custody records need control IDs, weights with the weighing-equipment identifier (to trace calibration), feedstock type (flexibles, rigids, PET, LDPE…), entity names and signatures, and dates of receipt, pre-processing and end-of-waste completion. None of these texts explicitly requires GPS or photos; both are cheap supporting evidence.

findings.point: India's mandatory plastic EPR can make collection non-additional, material by material. Every lot therefore needs a material type and a flag showing whether an EPR certificate was claimed.
findings.detail: PWRM0001 Step 1 (regulatory surplus) requires listing all relevant laws, including EPR schemes. Material types whose collection is mandatory are excluded unless enforcement is weak (compliance below 50%) or the project exceeds the mandated threshold. Its applicability conditions also require that: the sources are identifiable and would otherwise be dumped, openly burned or incinerated without energy recovery; and the output goes to an authorised destination that complies with local regulations. For Luma, that means checking the receiver's pollution-board consent. Khaitan notes that India's CCC rules say nothing about double counting with RECs. The same gap exists between CPCB EPR certificates, plastic credits and carbon credits on a single tonne.

findings.point: Timing and ownership rules decide whether pilot data can ever earn credits. Credit rights must be signed from day one, and validation completed within 2 years of the declared project start.
findings.detail: Verra Plastic Standard v1.0 (10 Feb 2021) sets these rules. The project start date is the day collection or recycling began. Projects starting on or after 1 Jan 2022 must complete validation within 2 years (4 years if they use a brand-new methodology). The crediting period is 7 years, renewable twice (21 years in total), or 10 years fixed. A grouped project can add new instances later, for example each kabadiwala or yard. Each new instance must lie inside the designated geographic area, meet the eligibility criteria and have ownership evidence dating from its own start; it earns credits from the next verification period. Ownership evidence means enforceable, irrevocable agreements or a contractual alliance. Records must be kept for at least 2 years after the crediting period ends. ICM offset projects need a start on or after 1 Jan 2025. GS 448 crediting may start up to 2 years before certification. A mid-October 2026 Bengaluru pilot fits all of these windows only if the paperwork starts now.

findings.point: The standards reward visibly better pay for informal workers, which gives Luma a direct design brief for revenue sharing with kabadiwalas and Saathis.
findings.detail: Verra Plastic Standard §3.14 requires: at least the regionally prevailing industry wage, while striving for a living wage; no withholding of wages as discipline; paid overtime; efforts to exclude under-18s, with strict conditions where they do work; and health and safety measures including PPE. Where a project displaces informal income, it must create alternatives that pay the same or more. Verra's program also offers labels for increased wages and safe work. PCX's qualitative additionality looks for higher wages or income, social security beyond the legal minimum, and inclusion of vulnerable groups. Plastic Bank's two-tier pay (cash at market rate, plus a digital bonus and social benefits) maps directly onto Luma's cash/UPI weigh-and-pay flow. Bengaluru already has a traceable-plastic player: Hasiru Dala Innovations sells blockchain-enabled, fully traceable post-consumer plastic under WFTO Fair Trade, with 327 supplier clients. It is a potential pilot partner or competitor.

findings.point: The SWM Rules 2026 create a national waste-tracking portal that is due about now. Luma's ledger should feed it rather than duplicate it.
findings.detail: The SWM Rules 2026 took effect on 1 Apr 2026. CPCB must launch a centralised online platform within six months, around 1 Oct 2026. It will track generation, collection, transport, processing and landfilling down to district level, based on self-reporting, and operating without registration draws fines. CSTEP, a Bengaluru think tank, says the rules fail to institutionalise informal workers. It recommends GPS-linked tracking, cross-verification and third-party audits, which are the same controls credit verifiers want. If one lot ledger produces both the portal exports and the VVB data room, nobody has to enter data twice.

findings.point: Internal gap: the v1 schema lets the platform mint carbon credits, and the privacy plan deletes photos after 90 days. Both clash with how credits actually work.
findings.detail: /Users/syedabdulmuqeeth/Developer/Luma.Green/convex/schema.ts defines carbonCredits minted from a settled trade, with statuses draft → pending_verification → issued → listed → transferred → retired, plus a creditTransfers table. Under every standard reviewed, only a registry issues credits, after third-party verification by a VVB or ACVA. The registries are Verra, Gold Standard, PCX, or BEE through the Grid-India registry. Luma can hold 'estimated' and 'credit-ready' quantities and mirror registry serial numbers, but it cannot create credits. /Users/syedabdulmuqeeth/Developer/Luma.Green/docs/operations/data-protection.md deletes household scrap photos after 90 days, while MRV records must survive at least 2 years after the crediting period. The fix is to make dispatch weigh slips, invoices and GRNs the evidence, and keep household data out of MRV. /Users/syedabdulmuqeeth/Developer/Luma.Green/docs/product/kabadiwala.md weighs household scrap in half-kilo steps. That is fine for payment, because PWRM0001 lets the credited weight be taken at dispatch.

recommendations.feature: Lot passport with a credit-readiness checklist (investor demo)
recommendations.why: Each seeded demo lot shows its journey household → kabadiwala → yard → recycler on a map. Alongside: weights, dates, weigh-slip photos, invoice and GRN, plus a checklist of the evidence each standard needs (Verra plastic, PCX, GS 448) and what is missing. This is what a verifier samples: PWRM0001 dispatch weights cross-checked with invoices and GRNs, and PCX chain-of-custody completeness. It makes 'credits later' a visible asset without claiming any credits now.

recommendations.feature: Honest impact counter that separates estimated, credit-ready and issued
recommendations.why: Replace the v1 idea of platform-minted carbonCredits (convex/schema.ts) with three numbers. First, kg diverted by material. Second, indicative tCO2e from a dated, sourced, admin-editable factor table, frozen per lot the way prices are. Third, credit-ready tonnes, meaning lots with complete evidence. Only registry serials (Verra, GS, PCX, or BEE via Grid-India) are ever called credits. This keeps the investor story accurate and avoids exposure to greenwashing complaints.

recommendations.feature: Green-bonus preview for kabadiwalas and Saathis
recommendations.why: Show the revenue-share rule as an effective-dated admin table, like the price floors. It splits net credit revenue between kabadiwala, Saathi, household points and Luma. Add an illustrative per-kg bonus at low and high prices ($106–$804/t), clearly marked 'not yet earned'. Verra and PCX reward visibly higher collector income, and Plastic Bank's cash-plus-bonus model fits Luma's UPI flow. This preview is also how pilot users will be persuaded to assign their credit rights.

recommendations.feature: Append-only lots and movements with two-sided receipts and a sorting mass balance
recommendations.why: The sender records the weight at dispatch; the receiver confirms its own weight (GRN) and the invoice. Yard sorting runs record input lots → graded output lots plus reject weight. Differences above a tolerance go to the admin. This meets PWRM0001/0002 monitoring, reuses the planned inventoryMovements with sort_out/sort_in, and blocks double claims.

recommendations.feature: Scale registry and weigh-slip capture at dispatch
recommendations.why: Each org lists its scales: ID, type, capacity, and Legal Metrology stamping or calibration date. Each dispatch picks a scale and attaches a photo of the display or weighbridge ticket, and lots weighed on out-of-date scales are marked not credit-ready. Verra requires calibration at least every 3 years, and PCX requires a weighing-equipment identifier. Because PWRM0001 allows measuring at dispatch, doorstep half-kilo weighing can stay as it is.

recommendations.feature: Credit rights, revenue share and a baseline declaration in onboarding
recommendations.why: Add a versioned clause in which each kabadiwala, yard, recycler and Saathi assigns the environmental attributes of Luma-recorded volume to Luma for pooled registration, in return for the published share. Add a declaration of the last 12–36 months' volume by material. Verra needs enforceable ownership evidence held from each instance's start date, and sets the capacity-addition baseline from the prior 3 years. Without these at pilot start, the pilot volume is lost for crediting.

recommendations.feature: One claim per lot, locked across EPR certificates, plastic credits and carbon credits
recommendations.why: Give each lot a claim status: none, EPR certificate number, reserved for a program, registry serial, or retired. ICM forbids concurrent registration with another carbon market, PCX credits transfer only once, and PWRM0001 treats materials under mandatory EPR as non-additional. India's rules are silent on double counting across instruments, so Luma has to enforce it itself.

recommendations.feature: Privacy-safe MRV evidence store with long retention
recommendations.why: In any MRV record, keep households pseudonymous and their location at ward or geohash-6 level. Keep weigh slips, invoices, GRNs, bale photos and SOP versions for at least 2 years after the crediting period (up to about 23 years). Store them apart from household photos, which keep their 90-day deletion. This meets Verra's records rules and DPDP-style data minimisation.

recommendations.feature: Work and pay log for Saathis and kabadiwala staff
recommendations.why: For each job, record who worked, hours, kg handled, pay, age-18 confirmation, and PPE and training. This is the evidence for Verra §3.14 safeguards: regional prevailing wage, a living-wage aim, no withheld wages, paid overtime and under-18 limits. It also meets PCX's income criteria and gives the payout base for revenue sharing.

recommendations.feature: Bengaluru grouped plastic-credit project, alone or with a partner developer
recommendations.why: Register the kabadiwala and yard network as one Verra Plastic Program grouped project: PWRM0001 for collection, PWRM0002 at partner recyclers, with each org added as an instance. Choose the start date deliberately, since validation must follow within 2 years. Consider partnering with an experienced Bengaluru player such as Hasiru Dala Innovations, which already sells traceable plastic, to reach first issuance faster. For plastics, per-tonne plastic credits pay far more than carbon credits.

recommendations.feature: Carbon-credit track for metals and for CCTS buyers
recommendations.why: Use the captured transport, energy and quality data to quantify carbon under GS 448 (metals) or VMR0007 (plastics, glass, aluminium, steel). Give obligated buyers (pulp & paper, aluminium including secondary, textiles, petrochemicals) documentation packs for their recycled inputs. Watch BEE for a recycling methodology in the Phase I waste sector.

recommendations.feature: Export to CPCB's SWM 2026 portal and the EPR portals from the same ledger
recommendations.why: The SWM Rules 2026 portal, due around 1 Oct 2026, tracks collection, transport and processing. Feeding both compliance reports and verifier data rooms from one ledger avoids double entry, and makes Luma hard for yards and recyclers to leave.

result.artifactMarkdown:
### Credit-ready ledger: fields to capture per transaction

**Transactions:**
- **T1** household pickup or drop-off (household → kabadiwala)
- **T2** dispatch between businesses (kabadiwala → yard → recycler → manufacturer)
- **T3** sorting run at a yard
- **T4** processing batch at a recycler
- **M** master data, captured once per org or person and referenced by every transaction

**Standards:**
- **V-PC** Verra PWRM0001 v1.1 (plastic collection)
- **V-PR** Verra PWRM0002 v1.1 (plastic recycling)
- **V-PS** Verra Plastic Standard v1.0
- **V-7** Verra VMR0007 with CDM AMS-III.AJ (carbon credits for HDPE, LDPE, PET, PVC, PP, container glass, aluminium, steel)
- **GS448** Gold Standard 448 v1.0 (carbon credits for metals, alloys, minerals)
- **PCX** PCX Plastic Pollution Reduction Standard v8
- **ICM** India's CCTS offset mechanism
- **SWM26** Solid Waste Management Rules 2026 (CPCB portal)

| # | Field (how to store) | When | Needed by | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Lot ID (immutable UUID) plus parent lot IDs | T1–T4 | PCX (control IDs; the verifier checks the full chain of custody) · V-PC (material reaches an end destination directly or through intermediaries) | Links every kilo from doorstep to recycler; one claim per lot |
| 2 | Event timestamps: collected, weighed, dispatched, received, processed (server and device time) | T1–T4 | V-PC (record every dispatch) · V-PR (each batch, at least daily) · PCX (dates of receipt, pre-processing, end-of-waste) · V-PS (project start = first collection; validate within 2 years) · ICM (project start on or after 1 Jan 2025) | Crediting windows and deadlines are set by dates |
| 3 | Material code mapped to a standard category: polymer (PET, HDPE, LDPE, PP, PVC, multilayer), form (rigid, flexible), paper grade, metal, glass cullet, EPR plastic category | T1–T4 | V-PC Step 1 (additionality tested per material type) · V-PR (material type i) · V-7 (eligible materials) · GS448 (material type i) · PCX (feedstock type) | Eligibility and additionality are decided material by material; paper has no active VCS or GS carbon methodology found |
| 4 | Gross, tare, deduction for moisture and contamination, net dry weight (integer grams) | T2–T4 (T1 for payment only) | V-PC (dry weight = weight minus non-plastic matter) · V-PR (washed plastic weighed after drying) · PCX (kg or t claimed) | This is the credited quantity |
| 5 | Scale ID, type (platform scale or weighbridge), capacity, Legal Metrology stamping or calibration date and certificate | M, used at T2–T4 | V-PC and V-PR (calibrate to the maker's specification or at least every 3 years) · PCX (weighing-equipment identifier to trace calibration) | Weights from an out-of-date scale cannot be credited |
| 6 | Weigh-slip or weighbridge ticket number, plus a photo of the slip or scale display (stored with a file hash) | T2–T4 | V-PC (direct measurement cross-checked with records) · PCX (documents the verifier reviews); the photo is supporting evidence, not named in the texts | Lets a verifier sample-check remotely |
| 7 | Sender org and receiver org (verified IDs); the receiver's goods receipt note (GRN) with its own weight and date | T2 | V-PC (weights cross-checked with invoices, payment receipts and GRNs from the end destination) · PCX (entity names, authorised signatures) | Two-sided confirmation is stronger than self-reporting and catches diversion or inflated weights |
| 8 | Invoice or receipt number, rate per kg, total, payment method and UPI reference (or cash) | T1–T2 | V-PC (invoice records, receipts of payment) · GS448 (weighed mass cross-checked with invoices or receipts) | The money trail corroborates the weight trail |
| 9 | Receiver's authorisations: pollution-board consent number, category and validity dates; SWM or CPCB registration; EPR processor registration | M, checked at each T2 | V-PC applicability 6–7 (authorised or licensed receiver that complies with local regulations) · SWM26 (registration; fines for operating without it) | Material sent to an unauthorised unit cannot be credited |
| 10 | Source type: household doorstep, household drop-off, shop or office, bulk generator, street or dump collection by a Saathi | T1 | V-PC applicability 3 (sources identifiable and otherwise dumped, openly burned or incinerated without energy recovery) | The core of the additionality case |
| 11 | Location: households at ward or geohash-6 only; org sites as exact lat/lng; device GPS and accuracy at each weighing | T1–T4 | V-PS (grouped-project instances inside a designated geographic area) · GS448 (transport distance per route) · SWM26 (district-level tracking); GPS itself is not mandated | Cheapest proof of where; coarse for household privacy |
| 12 | Transport: vehicle type, fuel, distance (from GPS or maps), trip ID | T2 | GS448 (transport emissions of waste and recyclates, per route) | Subtracted from carbon credits |
| 13 | Sorting run: input lot IDs and weights → output lots per grade, reject weight, hazardous items removed | T3 | V-PR (sorted output by material type, each batch, at least daily; hazardous material removed) · PCX (pre-processing date) | The mass balance proves what was actually recyclable |
| 14 | Processing batch: input lots, output product (flakes, granules, bales, ingots), output weight after the final stage, sale invoice to the final buyer | T4 | V-PR (inputs listed per batch; output weighed after the final stage and cross-checked with sales receipts) · GS448 (recyclate used downstream; downstream processing for leakage) | Recycling credits count output, not input |
| 15 | Quality: grade, contamination %, lab report if any | T3–T4 | GS448 (composition and quality set the substitution factor) · V-7 (discount for uncertain displacement of virgin material) | Decides how much virgin material counts as displaced |
| 16 | Facility energy: monthly kWh from meter or bill; diesel litres | M, monthly (yards, recyclers) | GS448 (electricity and fuel consumption) | Project emissions are deducted |
| 17 | Work record per job: Saathi or worker ID, role, hours, kg handled, pay, age-18 confirmation, PPE and training | T1–T3 | V-PS §3.14 (at least the regional prevailing wage, no withheld wages, overtime paid, limits under 18, health and safety) · PCX (higher wages, social security) | Safeguards evidence and the base for revenue-share payouts |
| 18 | Credit-rights consent: terms version accepted, timestamp, revenue-share rule version | M, at onboarding | V-PS §3.4 (enforceable, irrevocable agreement or contractual alliance) · V-PS grouped projects (ownership held from each instance's start date) | Without it the volume cannot be registered later |
| 19 | Claim status: none, EPR certificate number, reserved for a program, registry serial, retired | T2–T4 | ICM (no concurrent registration with another carbon market; Green Credit Programme excepted) · PCX (one transfer, then retired) · V-PC Step 1 (materials under mandatory EPR are not additional unless compliance is below 50%) | Blocks double counting across EPR, plastic and carbon credits |
| 20 | Baseline: each kabadiwala's and yard's pre-Luma monthly volume by material, with any evidence | M, at onboarding | V-PC Table 2b (capacity-addition baseline = maximum collection in the 3 years before; at least 1 year of data) | Only volume above the baseline is credited |
| 21 | Emission factor used (value, unit, source, version), frozen on the lot and shown as an estimate | T2–T4 | Luma's own rule (factors frozen like prices) · V-7 and GS448 recompute at verification (GS448 default baseline adjustment 99%, falling 1 point a year) | Honest investor numbers that never restate history |
| 22 | Audit trail: append-only rows, edit log (who, when, before, after), app version, file hashes; retained at least 2 years after the crediting period | all | V-PC §9.3 (electronic records, version control, QA/QC, SOPs, trained staff) · V-PS §3.17 (keep records 2+ years after the crediting period, about 23 years for a 21-year Verra plastic project) | This is what a verifier audits |

**Notes**
- Credits are counted at dispatch (T2) on a calibrated scale. Doorstep weights (half-kilo steps today) pay households and do not need to meet MRV standards.
- MRV exports never include a household's name, phone, exact address or photos. Household photos keep their 90-day deletion.
- Nothing above is a credit until a registry issues a serial number. Until then, show "estimated" and "credit-ready" quantities only.
risks: There is no Indian compliance route for recycling yet. None of the 8 ICM offset methodologies covers material recovery, offsets cannot be used for compliance, and CCC prices have not been discovered. Any 'Indian carbon credit' pitch for recycling is speculative until BEE adds a methodology.

Plastic-credit demand is thin and contested. Verra's program shows about 40,000 credits across 40+ projects worldwide, PCX prices span $106–$804/t, and PCX has paused 'net zero plastic' claims. Brand demand could stall.
Double counting: the same tonne could earn a CPCB EPR certificate, a plastic credit and a carbon credit. Under Verra, mandatory EPR can also make plastic collection non-additional.

Calling platform estimates 'credits', as the v1 carbonCredits table does, could mislead investors and buyers and draw misrepresentation or greenwashing complaints. This still needs checking against India's consumer-protection guidance on environmental claims.

Weight fraud would sink a verification: inflated weights, re-weighing the same bale, fake GRNs or uncalibrated scales. The defences are two-sided receipts, mass balance, calibration checks and anomaly alerts.
Privacy: keeping household GPS, addresses or photos for the long MRV retention period conflicts with DPDP minimisation and Luma's 90-day photo rule. Households have to stay out of MRV records.

Timing: Verra plastic projects must validate within 2 years of the declared start date, and ICM projects need a start on or after 1 Jan 2025. Choosing the wrong start date or missing the window forfeits early volume.

Social risk: if credit revenue stays with Luma or the yards instead of reaching kabadiwalas and Saathis, projects fail Verra's safeguards and the impact story collapses. SWM 2026 registration may also shut out unregistered informal collectors.
Cost: verifier audits and registry fees are largely fixed per verification. A handful of pilot testers will not produce enough tonnage to pay for them; quotes are needed.
openQuestions: Will BEE add a material-recovery or recycling methodology to the ICM offset mechanism (waste is a Phase I sector), and when?
What floor and forbearance prices will CERC approve for CCCs, and will offset CCCs ever count toward compliance?
Should Luma be the project proponent of a Verra grouped plastic project, or partner with an existing developer such as Hasiru Dala Innovations in Bengaluru?
What share of net credit revenue will kabadiwalas, yards and Saathis accept for assigning their credit rights, and should it be paid per kg after issuance or advanced earlier?
Can a tonne that generated a CPCB EPR certificate also earn a Verra WRC or WCC? This needs a legal opinion and a verifier's view.
Is paper or cardboard creditable under any active methodology? VMR0007 and GS 448, as read here, do not cover it.
What does a verification cost in India, and how many tonnes a year does it take for plastic credits to pay?
What will CPCB's SWM 2026 portal require of informal aggregators such as kabadiwalas, and can Luma report on their behalf?
Will a verifier accept ward- or geohash-level household location as evidence of an identifiable source?

result.headline: India's six live EPR regimes create certificates only from a registered recycler's records, which must be backed by invoices, entered in date order and capped at plant capacity. CPCB found about 7 lakh fake plastic certificates (38 times what recyclers could have produced), so verifiable chain-of-custody data starting at the kabadiwala is the missing layer Luma.Green can supply.

findings.point: Six EPR regimes are live, each on its own CPCB portal, and all work the same way: obligated producers buy certificates that only registered processors can generate.
findings.detail:
The six regimes:
- **Plastic packaging.** EPR Guidelines in Schedule II of the PWM Rules, 16 Feb 2022. Amended 14 Mar 2024 and again by GSR 237(E) on 31 Mar 2026.
- **E-waste, including solar PV.** GSR 801(E), in force 1 Apr 2023.
- **Batteries.** S.O. 3984(E), 22 Aug 2022.
- **Waste tyres.** HOWM Rules Schedule IX, GSR 593(E), 21 Jul 2022.
- **Used oil.** HOWM Rules Chapter VII, GSR 677(E) of 18 Sep 2023, in force 1 Apr 2024.
- **End-of-life vehicles (ELV).** S.O. 98(E), 6 Jan 2025, in force 1 Apr 2025.

In every regime, CPCB's portal creates certificates in the processor's name from the processor's own uploads of purchases, output and sales. Producers buy these certificates to meet their targets and file annual returns. If the producer's and the processor's figures differ, the lower one counts.

Portals: eprplastic.cpcb.gov.in, eprewaste.cpcb.gov.in, eprbattery.cpcb.gov.in, eprtyres.cpcb.gov.in, eprusedoil.cpcb.gov.in and eprelv.cpcb.gov.in.

findings.point: Kabadiwalas and yards do not register under any regime, except as used-oil collection agents. They appear in the records only as the seller on a recycler's purchase entry.
findings.detail:
How each regime treats collectors:
- **Plastic.** Only units that recycle, co-process, turn waste into energy or oil, or compost it register as Plastic Waste Processors (PWPs). Collectors do not register (CPCB FAQ).
- **E-waste.** Only manufacturers, producers, recyclers and refurbishers register; dismantlers and bulk consumers do not. Collection is formally limited to registered entities. Even so, a recycler buying from the informal sector may upload any receipt that shows the seller's name and address, and every seller's invoice must state the weight (CPCB FAQ, Jan 2024).
- **Tyres.** The recycler's purchase form asks for supplier name, address, domestic or import, tonnes, invoice number and date. The supplier's GSTIN is optional.
- **Batteries.** Anyone collecting or sorting waste batteries must hand them only to registered recyclers or refurbishers. The state pollution board (SPCB) can charge them environmental compensation (EC) for unsafe handling.
- **Used oil (the exception).** Collection agents must register on the portal, deliver only to registered recyclers, and file quarterly returns plus an annual return by 30 June.

findings.point: Certificates are created only from records that are backed by invoices, entered in date order and capped at capacity. Luma.Green's receipts and stock movements already have this append-only shape.
findings.detail:
- **E-waste recyclers** enter purchases first (by EEE item code, with invoices), then production, then end-product sales, strictly in date order. The portal rejects back-dated rows and allows no edits after saving. Output cannot exceed what was bought for each item code, and a year's purchases cannot exceed processing capacity. Sales invoices must be linked to GST.
- **Plastic PWPs** must upload a signed GST e-invoice for each sale before certificates are created. It must show buyer and seller GSTIN, IRN, date, HSN code, amount, invoice number and QR code, and it is checked against GSTN. Recycled tonnage may never exceed installed capacity, and certificates carry the unit's GST data.
- **Battery certificates** are also capped at installed capacity.
- **SPCBs** check capacity on site and review geo-tagged photos and videos of plants on the portal.

findings.point: Each regime counts certificates in a different unit, so Luma.Green's material catalogue needs a mapping to each regime with its conversion factors.
findings.detail:
- **Plastic:** tonnes, by category (I rigid, II flexible, III multilayer, IV compostable) and by type (recycling, end-of-life, recycled content, reuse). Issued in lots of 1 to 1,000 t and valid for 3 years from issue.
- **E-waste:** kg of iron, aluminium, copper or gold sold. Valid until 2 years after the end of the financial year in which it was created.
- **Batteries:** kg. CPCB's working method credits kg of key metal recovered and sold (lead, lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, zinc, copper, cadmium, aluminium, iron). The formula in the rules instead scales kg processed by actual recovery divided by the target recovery, and cuts imported feed by 20%. Valid 7 years.
- **Tyres:** credit = tonnes sold × conversion factor × weightage. Crumb rubber 1.333 × 1.0; reclaimed rubber 1.298 × 1.3; CRMB 0.2 × 1.1; recovered carbon black 3.676 × 1.25; pyrolysis oil and char 1.49 × 0.8 (continuous) or × 0.5 (batch). So 10 t of crumb rubber sold earns 13.33 t.
- **Used oil:** quantity × conversion factor × weightage (re-refined base oil 1.0, co-processing 0.25). Issued in lots of 100 to 10,000 kg.
- **ELV:** 1 kg of certificate per kg of steel scrap at a Registered Vehicle Scrapping Facility (RVSF). Valid 5 years.

findings.point: Targets rise steeply through 2028, so obligated producers need more verifiable post-consumer material every year.
findings.detail:
Targets for FY2026-27, with the next steps:
- **Plastic minimum recycling** (as a share of the EPR target): Cat I 70%, Cat II and III 50%, Cat IV 70%. From 2027-28 these become 80%, 60%, 60% and 80%.
- **Plastic recycled content:** Cat I packaging 40% this year, rising to 60% by 2028-29. Cat II is 10% and Cat III 5% this year, rising to 20% and 10% from 2027-28.
- **E-waste:** 70% of estimated waste generated, then 80% from 2027-28.
- **Batteries:** material recovery 90% for portable and EV batteries, 60% for automotive and industrial. Domestic recycled content 40% for automotive and industrial; for portable and EV it starts at 5% in 2027-28 and reaches 20% by 2030-31.
- **Tyres:** 100% of new tyres made or imported two years earlier.
- **Used oil:** 20% of base and lubricating oil sold in 2024-25, rising to 40% in 2028-29 and 50% from 2030-31.
- **ELV:** 8% of the steel in vehicles sold 20 years earlier (non-transport) or 15 years earlier (transport). This rises to 13% from 2030-31 and 18% from 2035-36.

findings.point: Certificate fraud is the system's biggest failure, and penalties now hit processors that over-claim.
findings.detail:
**What was found:**
- The Centre for Science and Environment (CSE, 30 Oct 2024) reported about 7 lakh fake plastic EPR certificates, 38 times what recyclers could actually have produced.
- ₹355 crore of environmental compensation was imposed.
- Co-processors claimed 335.4 million tonnes a year against 11.4 million tonnes of capacity.
- 41,577 producers, importers and brand owners were registered, with no virgin-plastic makers among them.
- The National Green Tribunal (NGT) took up the case on 26 Jul 2024 over about 6 lakh fake certificates from four recyclers, one of them in Karnataka.

**Penalties now in the rules:**
- Plastic processors that give false information are barred from the EPR system for 1 year.
- E-waste registrations can be revoked for up to 3 years, plus environmental compensation.
- Tyre or used-oil recyclers that over-claim by more than 5% of actual recycling face prosecution under section 15 of the Environment Protection Act (tyres) or revocation (used oil). For used oil, a third offence means permanent revocation.

findings.point: Most regimes now fix a certificate price band of 30–100% of the environmental compensation. The e-waste floor, reported at ₹22/kg, is being fought in the Delhi High Court.
findings.detail:
**Where the band applies.** The battery rules (GSR 190(E), 14 Mar 2024), tyre and used-oil rules (GSR 177(E), 12 Mar 2024) and ELV rules (rule 9(14)) all require CPCB to set a ceiling at 100% and a floor at 30% of the environmental compensation. Trades on the portal must fall inside that band.

**The e-waste dispute.** The 2024 e-waste amendment brought in a minimum price, reported at ₹22/kg. Blue Star, Havells, Daikin, Voltas, Samsung and LG are challenging it. In December 2025 the court paused, for Blue Star, CPCB's 12 December requirement that buyers and sellers declare they traded at or above the floor. The main case was still pending in January 2026.

**Late compliance.** Environmental compensation is partly refunded if a shortfall is cleared late:
- Plastic: 75%, 60% or 40% back if cleared within one, two or three years.
- Used oil: 85%, 60% or 30% back on the same timeline.

findings.point: A national exchange for EPR certificates is built but not yet approved, and it bans brokers. Luma.Green should supply it with data and material, not compete with it.
findings.detail:
**The design.** CPCB's guidelines for the EPR Electronic Trading & Settlement Platform (issued around Jan 2025) cover plastic, e-waste, batteries, tyres and used oil. Certificates are still created and transferred on the CPCB portals; pricing and payment move to the exchange. Key rules:
- A weekly uniform-price auction plus continuous trading.
- Floor and ceiling prices reset every quarter by CPCB.
- Payment through escrow.
- A 4% fee (2% from each side), of which 30% goes to CPCB.
- Prices and volumes published through an API.
- No brokers.
- Participants pay registration equal to 50% of the portal application fee, plus 25% of that each year.
- Direct trades by entities that are both an obligated entity and a processor are allowed for only 6 months after launch.

**Who may run it.** An operator needs at least ₹50 crore of annual platform revenue, ₹10 crore net worth, 10 years of experience and capacity for 50 lakh transactions a year.

**Status.** MSTC has built the platform, but approval was still pending in June 2026. Until then, certificates move between buyers and sellers directly on the portals.

findings.point: Checking is shifting to independent auditors. The 31 Mar 2026 plastic amendment lets Registered Environment Auditors verify compliance, and CPCB's guidelines for this are due around now.
findings.detail:
What GSR 237(E) changes:
- Plastic Waste Processors now include end-of-life processors.
- Turning plastic waste into feedstock chemicals or new plastic counts as recycling.
- Auditors registered under the Environment Audit Rules 2025 may verify compliance. CPCB has 6 months, roughly to the end of September 2026, to publish its verification guidelines.
- Brands may carry forward unmet 2025-26 food-contact recycled-content targets for 3 years, provided they clear at least a third each year.
- Recycled packaging must meet IS 14534:2023 and be labelled.
- Enforcement moves to local bodies, overseen by state committees chaired by Chief Secretaries.

E-waste and tyre certificates are already subject to environmental audit by CPCB or agencies it authorises.

findings.point: Filing deadlines change often, so they belong in editable data, not in code.
findings.detail:
**Standard deadlines:**
- E-waste, battery, tyre and used-oil recyclers file quarterly returns by the end of the month after each quarter.
- Plastic processors file annual returns by 30 April; producers, importers and brand owners by 30 June.
- RVSFs file quarterly Form 3 by the 30th of the next month.

**Extensions are routine:**
- The used-oil portal extended returns to 31 Mar 2026 (order of 23 Jan 2026), then moved FY2025-26 annual returns to 30 Nov 2026.
- The 2024 hazardous-waste amendment lets the Centre relax any return timeline by up to 9 months.

CPCB also asked the state boards on 15 Sep 2025 to physically inspect registered used-oil recyclers, and it issued a notice requiring GST e-invoices.

findings.point: Solar panels are covered by the e-waste rules but earn no tradable certificate today. The duty is to store waste modules until 2034-35.
findings.detail:
CPCB's e-waste FAQ says every maker and producer of solar PV modules, panels or cells must store the waste they generate up to 2034-35, following CPCB guidelines.

E-waste certificates exist only for iron, aluminium, copper and gold, plus refurbishing certificates by equipment code. The exchange's certificate list has no solar category.

For Luma.Green's planned solar module, this means recording where modules are routed and stored, not generating credits.

findings.point: Brands may legally pay for collection networks, and plastic certificates can be issued in a local body's name. That gives Luma.Green a way to earn from collection without selling certificates.
findings.detail:
**What brands may do.** The plastic guidelines let producers, importers and brand owners run deposit-refund, buy-back or similar schemes, and use voluntary collection points and third-party agencies.

**What they must still show.** Their 30 June annual return must include recycling certificates from registered processors only, and must name the recyclers they used.

**Local bodies.** A processor's certificate is issued in the name of a brand or a local authority, by agreement between them. The exchange lets local bodies sell certificates to brands. This matters for Bengaluru's municipal dry-waste network.

findings.point: In Karnataka, the state board (KSPCB) is the regulator Luma.Green's partners answer to, and it has already been caught up in a fake-certificate case.
findings.detail:
**KSPCB's role:**
- Plastic processors register with their state board through CPCB's central portal, and the state board charges them environmental compensation.
- Battery recyclers register with the state board. It can also charge anyone who collects or sorts batteries (kabadiwalas and yards included) for unsafe handling.
- State boards physically check e-waste and tyre recyclers' capacity.

**The Karnataka case.** The NGT's July 2024 notice named Enviro Recyclean Pvt Ltd of Karnataka among four recyclers accused of about 6 lakh fake certificates.

**What changes next.** The 2026 plastic amendment moves enforcement to local bodies, under a state committee chaired by the Chief Secretary.

**For the pilot.** Verified, auditable supply is a selling point to KSPCB-registered processors in Bengaluru.

recommendations.feature: EPR tag on every catalogue material: regime, category, unit and conversion factor, stored as dated data the admin can edit
recommendations.why: Certificates are counted per regime and category: plastic Cat I–IV in tonnes, e-waste and battery metal in kg, tyre credits with conversion factor × weightage, ELV steel in kg. CPCB revises these factors by notification. Add an eprMappings table keyed like priceFloors (materialId, regime, category, unit, factor, effectiveFrom). Every stock and lot screen can then show totals such as '1.2 t Cat I rigid this month', and a CPCB change needs no code change. It is cheap, visible in a demo, and every later EPR feature builds on it.

recommendations.feature: Lot passport: a QR-tagged bale or lot carrying its full chain of custody, with a one-click evidence pack
recommendations.why: After about 7 lakh fake plastic certificates, recyclers and brands need proof that tonnage exists and is post-consumer. Group the existing append-only pickup receipts and stock movements into lots or bales with a QR code, which the recycler scans on arrival. The lot's timeline (who, what, grams, when, where, photos, receipts) exports as a PDF or CSV evidence pack for state-board checks and Registered Environment Auditors. Demo it end to end with seed data: household pickup → kabadiwala → yard bale → recycler intake.

recommendations.feature: Exports that match the CPCB portals, for recyclers
Brand collection dashboard: kg collected by plastic category, city and lot, with links to the evidence
recommendations.why: The plastic guidelines let brands pay for buy-back or deposit-refund schemes and third-party collectors, while certificates must come from registered processors. Recycled-content duties (Cat I 40% this year, 60% by 2028-29) add demand for traceable recycled plastic. A mocked dashboard shows investors a revenue line: brands pay Luma.Green for verified collection, and partner processors issue the certificates. Luma.Green never trades certificates itself, which the national exchange forbids to brokers.

recommendations.feature: Receipt for sellers without a GSTIN
recommendations.why: For e-waste bought from informal sellers, CPCB accepts a receipt that names the seller and address and states the weight. Tyre purchase entries make the supplier's GSTIN optional. Issue a numbered, signed digital receipt for every kabadiwala → yard and yard → recycler sale: seller name, address, material, weight in grams, date, photo and a verification QR. This turns an informal trade into purchase evidence a recycler can upload.

recommendations.feature: GSTIN, e-invoice number (IRN) and e-way bill on business-to-business trades, plus recycled-content details on recycler → manufacturer orders
recommendations.why: Plastic certificates need a GST e-invoice for each sale, checked against GSTN, and e-waste and tyre certificates need GST-linked sales invoices. Add optional fields on yard → recycler and recycler → manufacturer trades: GSTIN (format-checked, then confirmed by the admin), IRN, e-way bill number and the invoice PDF. On recycler → manufacturer orders, also record polymer, category and recycled content, with IS 14534:2023 labelling. The recycler's certificate paperwork then starts on Luma.Green. This also answers open question 9 in kabadiwala-to-yard.md (what paperwork changes hands).

recommendations.feature: Capacity and date-order checks on the recycler's ledger
recommendations.why: The portals cap purchases and certificates at registered capacity and reject back-dated or edited entries. Over-claiming by more than 5% (tyres, used oil) is grounds for revocation or prosecution. Store each recycler's registered capacity per category (tonnes a year) from onboarding. Warn at 80% and 100% of the year's capacity. Keep ledger entries unchangeable, with corrections added as new linked entries.

recommendations.feature: Verified EPR registrations on business profiles
recommendations.why: Only registered processors can create certificates, and the battery rules make dealing with unregistered entities a violation. Onboarding already proposes a Plastic Waste Processor registration field. Extend it to every regime: e-waste recycler or refurbisher, battery recycler (state board), tyre recycler or retreader, used-oil recycler or collection agent, and vehicle scrapping facility. Capture the number, certificate PDF and expiry date, have the admin check them, and show a 'registered for …' badge. Kabadiwalas and yards then know where regulated materials may go.

recommendations.feature: Compliance calendar driven by editable rules, with SMS or WhatsApp reminders
recommendations.why: Deadlines move: used-oil FY2025-26 returns are now due 30 Nov 2026, and the Centre can relax any hazardous-waste timeline by up to 9 months. Price bands and floors are in court. Keep regimes, due dates, price bands, certificate validity and factors in one dated table the admin can edit. Remind recyclers and brands before quarterly returns (end of the following month) and annual returns (30 April for processors, 30 June for producers).

recommendations.feature: Routing rules for e-waste, batteries, used oil, tyres and solar modules
recommendations.why:
Each of these has a restricted path:
- E-waste may be collected only by registered producers, recyclers or refurbishers.
- Waste batteries must go to registered recyclers or refurbishers.
- Used oil may be collected only by registered collection agents.
- Solar modules go to the producer's storage until 2034-35.

When a household photo estimate or a kabadiwala stock line falls into one of these, route it to registered partners from the verified-registration list. Warn unregistered handlers and keep the item off the open marketplace.

recommendations.feature: Read-only EPR market prices from the national exchange
recommendations.why: The authorised exchange must publish prices, volumes and price history through an API. Showing weekly clearing prices by category helps recyclers value their feedstock and brands plan budgets. It keeps Luma.Green on the data side of the no-broker rule and can feed the planned live-prices module once MSTC's platform is approved.

- **Common to all:** CPCB's portal creates certificates in the processor's name from its uploads of purchases, output and sales. Producers buy them. If the two sides' figures differ, the lower one counts. Entries cannot be back-dated or edited.

risks: Liability for helping a violation: the used-oil rules let CPCB charge environmental compensation to any entity that aids or abets a violation, and the battery rules cover anyone who helps an obligated entity evade its duties. A platform whose inflated weights or unregistered routing feed false certificates could be pulled in, so records must be tamper-evident and anomalies flagged.

Positioning: the national EPR exchange allows no brokers, and running one requires at least ₹50 crore of annual platform revenue and 10 years of experience. Pitching Luma.Green as a 'credit marketplace' will not survive due diligence; position it as verified material and data.

Rule changes: the plastic rules were amended in 2022, 2024 and March 2026, deadlines are extended repeatedly, and the e-waste floor price is in court. Hard-coded factors, prices or dates will go out of date.

Legal grey zone for kabadiwalas: e-waste collection is limited to registered entities, used-oil collectors must register, and lead-acid batteries and used oil are hazardous. Openly helping unregistered handlers could draw KSPCB attention during the Bengaluru pilot.

GST friction: plastic certificates depend on GST e-invoices, which unregistered kabadiwalas cannot issue. Whether Luma.Green counts as a GST e-commerce operator is still an open question in the repo (question 12).

Privacy: receipts and evidence packs carry seller names, addresses and locations. Sharing them with recyclers and auditors needs notice, clear purpose and minimal data under the DPDP Act, and the packs must never be public.
No documented third-party API into the CPCB portals was found. Integration will be exports and manual uploads for the foreseeable future, so Luma.Green's value must not depend on automated filing.

Uncertain revenue: fraud drove certificate prices down, and prices are now set by price bands and court cases. Income from brand-funded collection will rise and fall with enforcement until the exchange and price floors settle.
openQuestions: Has MSTC's EPR trading platform been approved since June 2026, and when will direct buyer-to-seller transfers on the CPCB portals stop? A trade report (Enviliance, Apr 2026) says CPCB launched a common login portal, epr.cpcb.gov.in, in February 2026; this needs checking.

What evidence will CPCB's verification guidelines under the 31 Mar 2026 plastic amendment (due around September–October 2026) and Registered Environment Auditors accept? Could chain-of-custody records generated on a platform count as proof of post-consumer origin?
Does the plastic EPR portal accept receipts without GST for processors' purchases from informal collectors, as the e-waste portal does, or only GST e-invoices?

Trade sources list EPR regimes for non-ferrous metals and for construction and demolition waste as in force in 2026. Do they cover kabadiwala metal trades (copper, aluminium, brass), and who creates certificates there?
Do the Solid Waste Management Rules 2026, reported to be in force from 1 April 2026, require aggregators or scrap dealers to register on a portal?
What will the Delhi High Court finally rule on the e-waste floor price (reported at ₹22/kg), and will prices elsewhere be reset each quarter on the exchange?
Which KSPCB-registered plastic processors, e-waste recyclers and battery recyclers near Bengaluru would join a verified-feedstock pilot, and what documents do they ask yards for today?
Plastic certificates can be issued in a local authority's name. Should Luma.Green partner with Bengaluru's municipal dry-waste collection network?
