result.headline: India's customs tariff already uses ISRI grade names for scrap: 10 copper grades under 7404 00 12 and about 40 aluminium grades under 7602 00 10. So Luma.Green can publish a 60-code, two-tier catalogue that links doorstep words like raddi, gatta, Teri and Panni to 8-digit HSN lines, ISRI and IS 2549 grades and EPR categories, rather than inventing new grades.

findings.point: India's customs tariff already uses ISRI grade names for metal scrap
findings.detail: Tariff item 7404 00 12 (copper scrap) is defined by 10 ISRI code words: Barley, Berry, Birch, Candy, Cliff, Clove, Cobra, Cocoa, Dream and Palms. Item 7404 00 22 (brass scrap) names 25 code words, including Honey, Drink and Ocean. Item 7602 00 10 (aluminium scrap) names about 40, including Taint/Tabor, Tense, Troma, Zorba and the four used-beverage-can grades. Everything else goes to the 'other' lines 7404 00 19, 7404 00 29 and 7602 00 90. India's organised metal trade already works in ISRI terms, so Luma should cite ISRI code words for trade grades and not write its own metal definitions.

findings.point: The ISRI 2024 circular gives measurable limits that can become catalogue defaults
findings.detail: No. 2 copper (Birch/Cliff) has a nominal 96% copper content, 94% minimum. Taint/Tabor sheet aluminium allows at most 1% oil and grease and up to 10% painted siding. Tense (mixed castings) allows at most 2% oil and grease. Baled cans (Taldon) must be 225–273 kg/m3, and any free lead is grounds for rejection. HMS 1 means steel at least 1/4 inch (6.35 mm) thick in pieces no larger than 60 x 24 inches. HMS 2 means steel at least 1/8 inch (3.2 mm) thick, black or galvanised. For lead batteries, Rains means drained whole intact batteries and Rink means wet ones. The circular is copyrighted (2024 ISRI), so Luma should cite code words and numbers but write its own definitions.

findings.point: Ferrous scrap has an Indian standard, IS 2549:2023, and its HSN lines follow the grades traders use
findings.detail: The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) published its second revision of IS 2549, 'Processed ferrous scrap: code for classification', with effect from 26 Jan 2023. It classifies three kinds of scrap: prompt (from processing and manufacturing sites), obsolete (end of life) and home (from steel plants). It fixes definitions for HMS, shredded scrap and busheling. HSN 7204 splits into 7204 10 00 cast iron, 7204 21 90 stainless steel, 7204 30 00 tinned steel, 7204 41 00 turnings and stampings, and 7204 49 00 other (HMS and light melting scrap). Doorstep rate cards already split heavy from light iron: Rs 27 against Rs 22 per kg in Delhi.

findings.point: Paper has four HSN lines, a large import gap and poor sorting at source
findings.detail: HSN 4707 has exactly four lines: 10 00 unbleached kraft and corrugated (OCC), 20 00 bleached chemical pulp (white record, notebooks), 30 00 mechanical pulp (newspapers, magazines) and 90 00 other, including unsorted paper. A 2023 IPPTA review by FRI Dehradun reports that about 80% of Indian pulp comes from recovered paper. Yet India recovers only 25–28% of the paper it consumes, according to IARPMA, against a 58% global rate. About 20 Mt of demand is met by roughly 13 Mt collected at home and 7 Mt imported. Recovery by grade is 6.18 of 10.31 Mt for packaging, 2.87 of 7.18 Mt for writing and printing paper, and 1.84 of 2.63 Mt for newsprint. The review blames improper segregation, soiling and unsystematic baling, which is a direct case for standard grades at the kabadiwala.

findings.point: ISRI paper tolerances give ready-made quality defaults
findings.detail: Moisture: 12% is the maximum 'dry' limit, and the buyer can adjust the weight beyond it. In the limits below, 'prohibitives' are materials that make a bale unusable and 'outthrows' are papers that don't belong in the grade. OCC (#11): prohibitives at most 1%, outthrows plus prohibitives at most 5%. Double-sorted OCC (#12): 0.5% and 2%. Sorted office paper (#37): 1% and 5%. Mixed paper (#54): prohibitives at most 2%, outthrows at most 3%. Medical, food and hazardous waste are never tolerated. There is no weight adjustment when the two parties' scales differ by 1% or less on domestic loads. The EN 643 equivalents are OCC 1.05, double-sorted OCC 1.04 and sorted office paper 2.05.

findings.point: Every plastic has a street name, and colour and processing set the price
findings.detail: CSE's 2021 study of Delhi's informal market records these names: Teri for PET, Phugga for PP, Jhaap for HDPE, Kaala for black PP and HDPE, Kadak for PS and ABS, Panni for LDPE and PP film, and Jabla for HMPP sheets and bags. Scrap shops bought PET at Rs 22–32/kg, and its value rose from Rs 27 as bottles to Rs 39 as flakes, Rs 58 washed and Rs 65/kg as fibre. Colour does not change PET's price; the stream is 80% clear, 18% green and 2% blue. PP loses value in this order: transparent, white, coloured, mixed, black. HDPE ranks drum, transparent, crate, coloured, black. Multi-layer packets fetch only Rs 4–5/kg and end in waste-to-energy plants or cement kilns. So one PET code is enough, while PP and HDPE should be graded by colour at yard level.

findings.point: Plastic codes need the polymer (for HSN) and the EPR category (for brand owners)
findings.detail: India's tariff splits heading 3915 by polymer: 3915 10 00 PE, 20 00 PS, 30 10 and 30 90 PVC, 90 10 PP, 90 42 PET bottles and 90 90 other. The Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules 2026 (G.S.R. 237(E), 31 Mar 2026) require producers to use recycled content. For 2025-26 the targets are 30% for Category I (rigid), 10% for Category II (flexible) and 5% for Category III (multilayer). They rise to 60%, 20% and 10% by 2028-29, and the recycled plastic must conform to IS 14534:2023. Traceable post-consumer feedstock, tagged by EPR category, is therefore something brand owners will pay for.

findings.point: The GST rate depends on the HSN code: 5% for paper, glass and textiles; 18% for plastics, metals, e-waste and batteries
findings.detail: Notification 9/2025-Central Tax (Rate) was issued on 17 Sep 2025 and took effect on 22 Sep 2025. At 5% it lists recovered paper (4707), glass cullet (7001), worn clothing and rags (6309/6310), cotton waste, man-made fibre waste (5505) and rubber waste (4004 00 00). At 18% it lists plastic scrap (3915), ferrous (7204), copper (7404), aluminium (7602), lead (7802), zinc (7902), nickel and tin scrap, e-waste (8549, plus appliances discarded as e-waste), batteries (8506/8507) and used tyres (4012). Precious-metal waste (7112) is at 3%. Plastic scrap moved from 5% to 18% on 1 Oct 2021 under Notification 8/2021. Because rates change, they belong in a dated table keyed by HSN, not in the catalogue row.

findings.point: Metal scrap has its own tax rules, and they affect unregistered kabadiwalas
findings.detail: Since 10 Oct 2024, when an unregistered seller supplies metal scrap (Customs Tariff chapters 72–81) to a registered buyer, the buyer pays the 18% GST under reverse charge (Notification 06/2024-CT(Rate), 8 Oct 2024). Supplies between two registered parties above Rs 2.5 lakh carry a 2% GST TDS: 1% CGST plus 1% SGST (Notification 25/2024-CT, 9 Oct 2024). Luma's onboarding already records 'not GST-registered' for this reason, so every ferrous and non-ferrous code should carry a chapter 72–81 flag.

findings.point: E-waste and batteries are regulated streams, mostly priced per piece
findings.detail: In a letter dated 13 May 2024, CPCB lists 106 electrical and electronic items under the E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022, in seven groups: ITEW 1–27, CEEW 1–19, LSEEW 1–34, EETW 1–8, TLSEW 1–6, MDW 1–10 and LIW 1–2. The GST notification defines taxable e-waste by reference to the rules' schedule. The battery EPR rules cover every chemistry, and recyclers and refurbishers must register with both CPCB and the state pollution board. Those rules were amended in 2023, on 14 Mar and 20 Jun 2024, and on 24 Feb 2025. Doorstep rate cards in Delhi price appliances per piece, with variants: fridges at Rs 1,000, 1,500 or 1,800 for 1, 2 or 3 doors, ACs at Rs 3,500–5,000 for 1–2 ton, and LCD screens at Rs 200. Batteries go by weight, at Rs 80/kg.

findings.point: GST's unit codes already cover every unit used in the chain
findings.detail: The GST e-invoice master list includes KGS, QTL (quintal), MTS (metric ton), TON, NOS, PCS, BAL (bale), BDL, BAG and DOZ. That covers kilograms at the door, bales and tonnes at yards and mills, pieces for appliances and dozens for reusable bottles. If mass is stored in grams and each code has a pricing unit mapped to a UQC, receipts, delivery challans and later e-invoices stay consistent.

findings.point: Local names need care: dictionaries confirm some and contradict others
findings.detail: Dictionaries confirm these meanings: raddi means wastepaper or old newspapers (Marathi, and a Hindi synonym of kabaad); bhangar means scrap (Marathi); kabaad means junk or scrap (Hindi); gatta means cardboard (Hindi); aakri means scrap (Malayalam); attai means cardboard (Tamil). In Tamil, irumbu, cembu, eeyam and takaram are iron, copper, lead and tin. In Kannada, kabbina, tamra, hittale and gaaju are iron, copper, brass and glass. In Hindi, loha, peetal and seesa are iron, brass and lead. There are pitfalls. Hindi seesa (lead) sounds like sheesha (glass or mirror). The Kannada dictionary defines gujari as a small retail or evening market, not scrap, and rattu as book-cover board, not cardboard. Kannada raddi means refuse in general. Street usage has to be checked with Bengaluru kabadiwalas and stored as aliases, not as display names.

findings.point: Bengaluru evidence suggests about 40–60 codes, in two tiers
findings.detail: Saahas Zero Waste, based in Bengaluru, sorts dry waste into more than 40 categories. A secondary glossary says a skilled kabadiwala prices 30–50 streams by sight. A Delhi doorstep app lists about 22 per-kg lines and about 16 per-piece lines for appliances and vehicles. A household layer of about 20–30 codes that rolls up from about 60 trade and industrial grades matches how material is re-sorted at each hand-off.

findings.point: Grading is where the value is, as a Bengaluru example shows
findings.detail: Mongabay (May 2026) reports copper at Rs 1,000–1,200/kg in Padarayanapura, Bengaluru. A Delhi doorstep card pays Rs 550/kg for 'copper' and Rs 60/kg for copper cable. Chintan's formal channel raised the price of mixed small e-waste from Rs 40 to Rs 65/kg. A single 'copper' or 'e-waste' code hides that spread. Graded codes (bare bright, No. 2, insulated) let households and kabadiwalas see why prices differ.

findings.point: Glass is worth little unless it is colour-sorted or reused
findings.detail: Under ISRI, clear (flint) cullet must be 95–100% clear, with labels at most 0.2%, and no window glass, Pyrex, bulbs, mirrors or ceramics. Mixed glass from recovery facilities may contain at most 2% ceramics and 5% moisture, and no CRT glass at all. Glass bottles fetch only Rs 3/kg at the door in Delhi, and cullet (7001) is taxed at 5%. Whole bottles sold for refilling are a different product, sold per piece or per dozen.

recommendations.feature: Publish 'Luma Material Codes v0.1': the 60-code catalogue as a public page in 12 languages, with JSON and CSV downloads
recommendations.why: It gives investors a concrete standard-setting asset within weeks. Each code links doorstep words (raddi, gatta, Teri) to an 8-digit HSN line, ISRI or IS 2549 grades and an EPR category. It is data rather than a new user flow, so it is low-risk to build, and every later module (prices, stock, exchange, carbon) reuses it. Version it as 0.1.0, date every row, use an open licence (for example CC BY 4.0) and state that the tax columns are for information only.

recommendations.feature: Two-tier catalogue with roll-up: household, trade and industrial codes linked by parentCode, with sorting entries that move kilograms between them
recommendations.why: The brief says names and prices change at each hand-off. Households and the AI need about 20–30 simple codes; yards buy ISRI and IS 2549 grades. The planned sorting entry then reads 'PAP-MIX 50 kg becomes PAP-ONP 30 + PAP-OCC 15 + reject 5', which makes a clear traceability demo.

recommendations.feature: Catalogue schema in Convex: immutable ASCII codes (3-letter family plus grade, for example PAP-OCC), with GST rates and CO2e factors kept in separate dated tables
recommendations.why: The fields are: code, family, level, parentCode, messageKey, aliases per locale, hsn, unit and UQC, typicalGramsPerPiece, variants, and references (ISRI code words, IS 2549 grade, EN 643 grade, EPR category, resin code, e-waste schedule code, battery type). Add quality defaults (moisture, prohibitives, outthrows, metal content, oil), flags (shown to the AI, metal scrap under chapters 72–81, regulated e-waste or battery, low value), icon, colour, active, replacedBy and catalogue version. The families would be paper, plastic, ferrous, nonferrous, glass, ewaste, battery, textile and other. Splitting metal into ferrous and non-ferrous and adding battery matches how buyers, tax (reverse charge only for chapters 72–81) and rules differ. Dated rate and factor tables follow ADR 0008, so a rate change never rewrites a receipt. One seed JSON file in the repo, plus admin editing of names, aliases and active flags, keeps the data easy to change.

recommendations.feature: Limit the AI estimate to about 20 household codes it can recognise in a photo, and have it return a 'we don't buy / low value' list (thermocol, multi-layer packets, food-soiled paper)
recommendations.why: A smaller set of answers should score better on the labelled photo set. Multi-layer packets fetch only Rs 4–5/kg, and food or medical waste is never accepted in paper bales, so households should be told early.

recommendations.feature: Bengaluru name-collection sprint: record the words 10 pilot kabadiwalas actually use for each code, in Kannada, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu and Hindi, with short voice clips
recommendations.why: Dictionaries contradict street usage (gujari, rattu), Delhi plastic slang may not be used in Bengaluru, and sound-alikes such as seesa (lead) and sheesha (glass) are a real risk when the app reads requests aloud. The collected words become aliases for search and the speaker button; display names stay hand-translated.

recommendations.feature: Per-piece e-waste and battery codes, with variants (fridge doors, AC tonnage, battery type) and a typical weight per piece measured during the pilot
recommendations.why: Appliances are priced per piece at the door (fridges Rs 1,000–1,800, ACs Rs 3,500–5,000), but stock, carbon and EPR reporting need kilograms. Recording both from day one avoids a later migration.

recommendations.feature: Quality and deduction lines at the kabadiwala-to-yard hand-off (moisture %, contamination %, recovery %), pre-filled from catalogue defaults such as 12% moisture for paper and the ISRI limits for OCC
recommendations.why: Weight is the source of truth, and deductions are where disputes and trust are decided. Standard defaults make prices comparable across yards and later feed the escrow module.

recommendations.feature: Tax-aware records: print the HSN code and unit code on receipts and delivery challans, and for ferrous and non-ferrous codes sold by an unregistered kabadiwala to a registered yard, show 'GST payable by buyer under reverse charge'
recommendations.why: Yards have needed these facts since 10 Oct 2024. Recording them without filing anything fits ADR 0009 (money off-platform first) and makes Luma useful to GST-registered buyers.

recommendations.feature: Route regulated streams: e-waste and battery codes can be offered only to businesses whose CPCB or state-board recycler or refurbisher registration the admin has verified
recommendations.why: The e-waste and battery rules require registered recyclers and refurbishers. Routing by code keeps Luma from facilitating illegal dismantling, and it becomes a trust feature.

recommendations.feature: EPR traceability export: tag each plastics lot with its EPR category, resin code and post-consumer origin, from household code to recycler output (for example PLA-PET to PLA-PET-FLAKE)
recommendations.why: Recycled-content targets reach 60% for Category I by 2028-29, so brand owners and processors need traceable feedstock. The same pattern later serves e-waste and battery EPR and carbon credits.

recommendations.feature: Run the catalogue as an open standard: public change requests, semantic versioning, codes never reused, maintained crosswalks (HSN, ISRI, EN 643, IS 2549, e-waste schedule, battery categories), and an invitation to trade bodies such as IARPMA
recommendations.why: The industry will adopt the codes only if they are stable and neutral. Tariffs and rules keep changing (GST in 2021 and 2025, plastic rules 2022–2026), so the crosswalks need a scheduled review.

## Luma Material Codes (LMC): proposed v0.1 catalogue (60 codes)

**How to read it**

- **Code**: 3-letter family plus a grade token, in ASCII. Codes are never renamed or reused; a retired code points to its replacement (`replacedBy`).
- **Level**: H = household (doorstep and AI photo estimate), T = trade (kabadiwala sorts for the yard), I = industrial (recycler output).
- **HSN**: the Indian tariff item. It is 8-digit where checked against the ITC-HS schedule; where it wasn't checked, it is 4- or 6-digit and marked (tbc).
- **Unit**: the pricing unit, with its GST unit code (kg = KGS, piece = NOS, dozen = DOZ, bale = BAL, tonne = MTS). Mass is always stored in grams.
- **Trade names**: hi Hindi, mr Marathi, kn Kannada, ta Tamil, gu Gujarati. *Delhi* = names recorded by CSE (2021) in Delhi's informal plastics market. † = meaning checked in Wiktionary, the Alar dictionary or CSE; (tbc) = to confirm with the Bengaluru pilot kabadiwalas. Display names in all 12 languages come from `messages/*.json`; these trade names are search and voice aliases.
- **ISRI** = code words and paper grade numbers from the ISRI (now ReMA) Scrap Specifications Circular 2024.

risks: Publishing HSN and GST columns invites people to rely on them for tax filings. A wrong 8-digit line could cause misclassification, and the 7001, 7802 and 8549 sub-lines are not yet checked. Mark these columns as for information only, date every row and have the admin review them.

ISRI specifications are copyrighted (2024 ISRI). Reproducing their definitions in a public standard could draw objections, so cite the code words (which India's own tariff uses) and write original definitions.

E-waste and battery handling by unregistered kabadiwalas is restricted. A marketplace that lists these items without routing them to registered recyclers could be seen as facilitating illegal dismantling.
A wrong or offensive local name (seesa for lead vs sheesha for glass, or gujari) would erode trust with low-literacy users, and Delhi plastic slang may mislead in Bengaluru.
There is a granularity trade-off. Too many codes overwhelm kabadiwalas and the AI; too few hide price spreads (copper at Rs 550 vs over Rs 1,000/kg) and mislead households.
Rules keep changing: GST in 2021 and 2025, plastic rules from 2022 to 2026, battery rules from 2023 to 2025. Without dated tables and a review schedule, static data will go out of date.
Renaming or reusing codes would corrupt receipts, stock history and EPR or carbon claims, so codes must be immutable.
Showing reverse-charge and TDS facts may push informal traders to under-record transactions, or create an expectation that Luma gives tax advice.
openQuestions: What are the exact 8-digit lines for glass (7001 00 xx), lead (7802 00 xx), the 8549 sub-headings (lithium-ion, dry cells, CRT glass, circuit boards), 6309/6310 and reusable bottles (7010)? Confirm against the CBIC tariff before publishing.
Which e-waste schedule item codes (the ITEW, CEEW and LSEEW numbers) match each appliance code? This needs the official schedule text.
What words do Bengaluru kabadiwalas use for plastics: Delhi's Teri, Phugga, Jhaap and Panni, English PET, PP, HD and LD, or Kannada terms? Are milk pouches (Nandini) a separate paid stream?
Is 'gujari' used for scrap shops in Bengaluru, given that the dictionary defines it as a small retail or evening market?
Should small appliances and fans be priced per kg (Delhi cards pay Rs 25/kg for fans) or per piece?
Will the pilot show tax facts at all, given that ADR 0009 keeps money off-platform first?
Did new national solid-waste rules (reported for 2026, not verified here) add a separate household stream for hazardous items that should own batteries and bulbs?
Who owns the standard in the long term (Luma alone or a group of industry partners), and under which licence?
Which source should supply the emission factor for each code? That is for the carbon module's research.

result.headline: Keeping money off the platform (ADR 0009) keeps Luma.Green outside GST e-commerce TCS and RBI payment-aggregator licensing for the Bengaluru pilot. Escrow would switch both on: 0.5% TCS with a GSTR-8 due by the 10th of every month, and money could only be held by an RBI-authorised aggregator, which itself needs ₹15 crore net worth. The amended E-Commerce Rules add grievance, seller-disclosure and dark-pattern-audit duties from 1 Jan 2027 whether or not escrow ever starts.

findings.point: Metal scrap has its own GST paperwork since 10 Oct 2024, and the right document depends on whether the seller is GST-registered
findings.detail: Notification 06/2024-CT(Rate) (8 Oct 2024, in force 10 Oct 2024) put metal scrap of Customs Tariff chapters 72–81 under reverse charge when an unregistered person sells to a registered one. The buying yard pays the GST, and CGST s.24(iii) makes anyone liable under reverse charge register. New Rule 47A (Notification 20/2024-CT, from 1 Nov 2024) requires the buyer to issue that self-invoice within 30 days of receiving the goods. When both sides are registered, Notification 25/2024-CT with s.51 makes the buyer deduct GST TDS of 1% CGST plus 1% SGST (2% in all) once the contract value exceeds ₹2.5 lakh. No deduction applies where the supplier's location and place of supply are in another state. The buyer deposits the TDS and files GSTR-7 by the 10th, and registers as a deductor through form REG-07 as 'Metal Scrap Dealers' (GSTN advisory, 22 Oct 2024). Luma.Green's onboarding already records 'Not GST-registered' explicitly, and that flag is what decides which document applies. This also answers the docs' open question 3: a yard or recycler that buys metal from unregistered kabadiwalas has to be GST-registered.

findings.point: Households are outside GST, and most kabadiwalas are below the ₹40 lakh registration line
findings.detail: Under GST, a 'supply' is one made in the course or furtherance of business (CGST s.7). A family selling its own old newspapers therefore needs only a receipt, not a tax invoice. Suppliers of goods only must register once all-India aggregate turnover passes ₹40 lakh. The limit is ₹20 lakh in ten listed states, and Karnataka is not one of them. Suppliers of services or mixed supplies register above ₹20 lakh. The October 2024 reverse-charge entry names metal scrap only, so paper and plastic bought from unregistered kabadiwalas are not caught by it.

findings.point: Luma.Green only becomes a GST e-commerce operator that must collect 0.5% TCS once it collects the money
findings.detail: Anyone who runs a digital platform for e-commerce is an e-commerce operator (ECO) under s.2(45), as the CBIC FAQ explains. Section 52 TCS, however, applies only 'where the consideration … is to be collected by the operator'. The rate has been 0.25% CGST plus 0.25% SGST (0.5% IGST between states) since 10 Jul 2024 (Notification 15/2024-CT). Registration regardless of turnover applies only to an ECO required to collect TCS (s.24(x), since 1 Feb 2019). Such an ECO pays the TCS and files GSTR-8 within 10 days of each month-end, plus an annual statement before 31 December. Sellers supplying through a TCS-collecting ECO must register (s.24(ix)). The exception is intra-state goods sellers below the threshold who take a PAN-based enrolment number instead (Notification 34/2023-CT, from 1 Oct 2023). With ADR 0009 the pilot stays outside TCS, and escrow would switch all of this on.

findings.point: E-invoicing starts at ₹5 crore turnover and e-way bills at ₹50,000 per load, but handcarts and cycles are exempt
findings.detail: E-invoices (an IRN for each invoice) are mandatory for businesses whose aggregate turnover exceeded ₹5 crore in any year since 2017-18 (Notification 10/2023-CT, from 1 Aug 2023). That affects large yards, recyclers and manufacturers. Rule 138 requires an e-way bill before goods worth more than ₹50,000 move. This includes a registered buyer's inward load from an unregistered seller, which the registered buyer must generate. Goods carried by non-motorised conveyance need no e-way bill (r.138(14)(b)), which covers the kabadiwala's handcart or cycle. An e-commerce operator may fill Part A on the consignor's authorisation. Part B can be skipped for moves of up to 50 km to a transporter. Validity is one day per 200 km and can be extended within 8 hours of expiry.

findings.point: Income tax adds TCS on scrap sales (2% from 1 Apr 2026) and a 0.1% TDS on e-commerce operators
findings.detail: Budget 2026-27 proposed raising the TCS that a seller collects on scrap from 1% to 2% under s.394(1) of the Income-tax Act 2025, effective 1 April 2026 (Finance Bill memorandum, clause 73). Separately, s.194-O of the 1961 Act requires e-commerce operators to deduct TDS on sales they facilitate; the rate was cut from 1% to 0.1% from 1 Oct 2024. Whether this e-commerce TDS applies to Luma.Green while buyers pay sellers directly needs a tax adviser's answer before business-to-business trades go live.

findings.point: The E-Commerce Rules were amended on 9 Sep 2026, and the new duties apply from 1 Jan 2027
Because it hosts listings, photos and reviews, Luma.Green is an intermediary with IT Rules 2021 duties
DPDP Rules 2025: the core duties start around 13 May 2027, and breaches must be reported to the Board within 72 hours
findings.detail: G.S.R. 846(E) of 13 Nov 2025 set three start dates: the Data Protection Board rules immediately, the consent-manager rule after one year (about 13 Nov 2026), and notices, security, breach, retention and rights (rules 3, 5–16, 22–23) after 18 months. Security safeguards include encryption or masking, access control and logs kept for one year. Personal data, traffic data and processing logs must be kept for at least one year (r.8(3)). A breach must be told to each affected person without delay and reported to the Board in detail within 72 hours. Rights requests must be answered within 90 days. Penalties reach ₹250 crore for security failures, ₹200 crore for missed breach notices or children's data, and ₹50 crore for anything else. The repo's data-protection page already plans to this standard, with a 30-day target for rights requests.

findings.point: Holding trade money would make Luma.Green a payment aggregator, which needs RBI authorisation and ₹15 crore net worth
findings.detail:
RBI's Master Direction of 15 Sep 2025 (RBI/DPSS/2025-26/141) sets these rules:
- Anyone aggregating payments for merchants needs RBI authorisation, with ₹15 crore net worth at application and ₹25 crore by the end of its third year.
- A payment aggregator may not run a marketplace itself.
- Merchant money sits in an escrow account at a scheduled commercial bank, and that account may not be used for cash on delivery.
- An aggregator must stop a marketplace from taking payments for sellers not onboarded on that marketplace.
- Merchants with turnover up to ₹40 lakh can be onboarded with PAN or Form 60, a physical check of the shop and one officially valid ID document.
The practical route is a licensed aggregator's marketplace (split-payment) product, never Luma.Green's own bank or UPI account.

findings.point: Every scale used in trade must be verified by Legal Metrology, and electronic scales must be re-verified every 12 months
findings.detail: Rule 27 of the Legal Metrology (General) Rules 2011 says every weight or measure used in a transaction must be verified and stamped by the state's Legal Metrology officer. Re-verification is due every 24 months for weights and beam scales, and every 12 months for other instruments such as electronic platform scales and weighbridges. Using an unverified weight is punishable under s.33 with a first-offence fine of ₹2,000–₹10,000 and up to a year in jail for repeat offences, as listed by Invest Karnataka in Sep 2025. DoCA brought Jan Vishwas amendments to the Legal Metrology Act into force from 1 May 2026 (S.O. 2103(E)). The 2026 Jan Vishwas Bill, passed on 2 Apr 2026, adds improvement notices for first offences, so the current penalty should be re-checked.

findings.point: In Karnataka, a unit's pollution category decides whether it needs a KSPCB consent and for how long
findings.detail:
KSPCB, the Karnataka pollution board, sorts units into Red, Orange, Green and White categories (list per its notification of 27 Jul 2020). Consents are valid 5 years for Red and Orange and 10 years for Green (notification 1425 of 15 Jun 2016). Entries relevant to scrap:
- Orange: waste-plastic reprocessing; aluminium or copper recovery from scrap in oil-fired furnaces; end-of-life vehicle and scrap dismantling or shredding centres.
- Red: recycling hazardous scrap such as lead-acid battery plates and e-waste components.
- White ('not included in the consent mechanism'): hydraulic baling of waste paper.
KSPCB's public XGN register lists every consent with the unit, category colour, consent number and validity date, so the admin can check each claim. In Bengaluru, trade licences are issued online by the Greater Bengaluru Authority. Its portal was down for migration from 21 to 24 Sep 2026.

findings.point: Saathi work probably makes Luma.Green an 'aggregator' under both the central Social Security Code and Karnataka's 2025 gig-workers law
findings.detail: The Code on Social Security came into force on 21 Nov 2025. Aggregators owe 1–2% of annual turnover, capped at 5% of what they pay workers, but no rate has been notified yet. The Social Security (Central) Rules of 8 May 2026 require aggregators to register on the Shram Suvidha portal, upload existing gig workers within 45 days and report joins and exits in real time. Workers qualify for benefits after 90 days with one aggregator or 120 days across several. Karnataka's Act requires aggregators to register with its welfare board within 45 days and pay a welfare fee of 1–5% of each payout. In Feb 2026 the fee was set at 1% with per-transaction caps; for e-marketplaces the caps are ₹0.50 for two-wheelers, ₹0.75 for three-wheelers and ₹1.00 for light commercial vehicles, declared quarterly. Contracts must state pay terms and the right to refuse tasks. Deactivation needs 14 days' notice with reasons, disputes go to an internal committee that must act within 14 days, and fines run from ₹5,000 to ₹1 lakh plus 12% a year interest on unpaid fees.

findings.point: Buyers must pay micro and small suppliers within 45 days
findings.detail: Under the MSMED Act s.16, as summarised on the MSME Samadhaan portal, a buyer that pays a Udyam-registered micro or small supplier more than 45 days after accepting the goods owes compound interest with monthly rests at three times the RBI bank rate. Many recyclers are small enterprises, so invoice due dates and any future escrow release should respect the 45-day limit.

recommendations.feature: Rulebook: every legal threshold, rate and deadline stored as data the admin can edit, each with an effective-from date. This covers the ₹50,000 e-way bill limit, the ₹2.5 lakh limit and 2% rate for GST TDS, ₹5 crore for e-invoicing, ₹40 lakh for GST registration, 0.5% e-commerce TCS, 2% TCS on scrap, 12- or 24-month scale re-verification, 5- or 10-year consent validity and the gig-fee caps

Auto-invoices that pick the right document for each hand-off from the seller's GST flag and the material code: a household receipt, an RCM self-invoice with payment voucher, a tax invoice with a 2% TDS note, a TCS line, and later an IRN (e-invoice) through a GST provider
recommendations.why:
The documents differ at each step:
- Household to kabadiwala needs only a receipt, because it is not a business supply (CGST s.7).
- An unregistered kabadiwala selling metal to a registered yard needs the yard's reverse-charge self-invoice within 30 days.
- Metal between two registered parties above ₹2.5 lakh needs 2% GST TDS.
- Scrap sales carry income-tax TCS, 2% from 1 Apr 2026.
- From 1 Jan 2027 the seller's name must appear in the same font size as the platform's.
Getting this right automatically removes a common scrap-trade tax error and makes a strong investor demo. It also settles the docs' open question: require a GSTIN from any yard, recycler or manufacturer that buys metal.

recommendations.feature: Weighing-scale records: for each scale, its type and capacity, Legal Metrology certificate number, stamp photo and next due date, with a reminder 30 days ahead, a 'Scale verified until …' badge on booking, and a photo of the reading on every weigh-and-pay
recommendations.why: Every scale used in trade must be verified and stamped. Electronic scales and weighbridges are re-verified every 12 months and beam scales every 24. An unverified scale drew a ₹2,000–₹10,000 fine on a first offence, and since 1 May 2026 improvement notices come first. A visible verified scale is the strongest proof of the fair price that households are promised.

recommendations.feature: E-way bill helper: a yes/no checker (value, vehicle type, registration status, distance), then Part A pre-filled from the trade record for the portal, and later a GST-provider API
recommendations.why: Rule 138 requires an e-way bill for motor-vehicle loads over ₹50,000, including a registered buyer's inward load from an unregistered seller. Handcarts and cycles are exempt. An e-commerce operator may fill Part A on the consignor's authorisation, and each bill is valid for one day per 200 km, so the helper can also show a countdown.

recommendations.feature: Document vault and public compliance passport: the GSTIN (checked on the GST portal), KSPCB consent with colour, number and validity (checked on XGN), trade licence, Udyam, CPCB EPR registrations and PAN, shown as badges such as 'Consent valid till 2031' or 'GST verified'
recommendations.why: KSPCB consents run 5 years (Red and Orange) or 10 years (Green) and can be checked publicly on XGN. From 1 Jan 2027 sellers must disclose a GSTIN or Udyam number. RBI's small-merchant KYC for escrow needs PAN, a shop check and one ID. The vault turns the admin's manual checks into a visible trust signal for investors and buyers, and most of the data is already collected in onboarding.

recommendations.feature: Compliance calendar per organisation: GSTR-7 and GSTR-8 by the 10th, consent expiry 30 days ahead, scale re-verification, trade licence renewal, the quarterly Karnataka gig-welfare fee, 45-day payment deadlines to micro and small suppliers, and the yearly dark-pattern self-audit
recommendations.why: Most penalties in this sector come from missed dates rather than wrong rates. Examples: the TDS return by the 10th, consents lapsing after 5 or 10 years, 12-month scale re-verification, compound interest at three times the bank rate after 45 days, and quarterly gig fees. Reminders built on the Rulebook cost little once it exists.

recommendations.feature: Grievance desk and a pack of legal pages: a named Grievance Officer, a ticket system with 24-hour and 48-hour acknowledgement timers, the legal name and address block, a ranking explanation, sponsored labels, the National Consumer Helpline convergence application, terms in English and Eighth-Schedule languages, and a yearly reminder to users
recommendations.why: The IT Rules require acknowledgement within 24 hours and resolution within 15 days. The E-Commerce Rules require acknowledgement within 48 hours, a copy of the complaint and redress within one month. The 2026 amendment makes the National Consumer Helpline convergence programme, address disclosure and the dark-pattern certificate mandatory from 1 Jan 2027. These pages need to exist before real users arrive.

recommendations.feature: Saathi work register and gig-law pack: days worked per engager, joins and exits, payouts recorded, export for Shram Suvidha and the Karnataka welfare board, a welfare-fee calculator (1%, capped per vehicle type), and a Saathi agreement covering pay basis, the right to refuse tasks, 14 days' notice and a dispute flow
recommendations.why: The central rules of 8 May 2026 require aggregators to register, upload workers within 45 days and report joins and exits in real time, with benefits after 90 or 120 days of work. Karnataka requires board registration within 45 days and a 1% fee capped at ₹0.50–₹1.00 per e-marketplace job, paid quarterly. Its fines run ₹5,000–₹1 lakh plus 12% interest.

recommendations.feature: Escrow only through an RBI-authorised payment aggregator's marketplace (split-payment) product, with an 'e-commerce operator switch' that turns on TCS collection, the GSTR-8 export and seller registration or enrolment checks
recommendations.why: Licensing itself as a payment aggregator needs ₹15 crore net worth, rising to ₹25 crore. Aggregators cannot run marketplaces, and a marketplace may only take payments for onboarded sellers. Escrow also makes Luma.Green a GST e-commerce operator: 0.5% TCS, GSTR-8 by the 10th and an annual statement by 31 Dec. Sellers would then need GST registration or a PAN-based enrolment number, which is limited to intra-state sales. The pilot should keep only recording payments, and households and small kabadiwalas should stay out of escrow.

recommendations.feature: Privacy centre ready for DPDP: a notice for each role, a consent log, rights requests (30-day target, 90-day legal limit), a breach runbook (CERT-In within 6 hours, the Board within 72 hours) and log retention of at least one year
recommendations.why: The core DPDP duties apply from about 13 May 2027 and penalties reach ₹250 crore. Building to the standard now, as the repo's data-protection page already plans, avoids a rebuild and reassures investors.

recommendations.feature: Provenance and prohibited-items guard: a booking checklist and photo review that flags utility cables, manhole covers, lead-acid batteries and e-waste; hazardous categories sent only to authorised recyclers; the seller's phone, photos and weight kept for each purchase; matching terms in the user agreement
recommendations.why: The IT Rules require the user agreement to bar unlawful content. In Karnataka, recycling lead-acid battery plates and e-waste components is a Red-category activity. Stolen metal is the trade's best-known legal risk. A purchase trail protects honest kabadiwalas and the platform.

risks: Escrow switches on several regimes at once. Funds must go through an RBI-authorised aggregator. Luma.Green must register for GST as an e-commerce operator, collect 0.5% TCS and file GSTR-8 monthly. Sellers must be GST-registered or enrolled with their PAN. E-commerce TDS may also apply. Together these could push unregistered kabadiwalas off the platform, so households and small kabadiwalas should stay outside escrow.
Receiving any trade money into Luma.Green's own bank or UPI account, even briefly, looks like unauthorised payment aggregation, and authorisation needs ₹15 crore net worth.
A 'Verified scale' badge will show that many kabadiwala scales are unstamped. Making it a hard requirement in the pilot could empty the supply side, so treat it as a nudge with a deadline.

Stolen or hazardous scrap (utility cables, manhole covers, lead-acid batteries, e-waste) passing through the platform exposes users to charges of receiving stolen goods and to pollution law, and exposes Luma.Green to reputational damage.

Saathi classification is uncertain. If Luma.Green counts as an 'aggregator', central registration (within 45 days) and Karnataka welfare-fee duties apply even though kabadiwalas pay the Saathis. Misjudging this risks fines of ₹5,000–₹1 lakh plus 12% interest.
AI price estimates shown to households could be treated as misleading if the final weighed prices are routinely lower. Label estimates clearly and publish their accuracy.
Hard-coded thresholds will go out of date: at least six legal numbers changed between Jul 2024 and Jan 2027.

DPDP penalties reach ₹250 crore. Household photos sent to an overseas model provider and data hosted in the EU need named processors, contracts, and logs kept for one year. MeitY has also considered shortening deadlines for some companies.
Binding legal text in 12 languages invites translation errors. Arabic is not an Eighth-Schedule language, so the binding version should be English or an Eighth-Schedule language.
Investor demos must not use real GSTINs, consent numbers or business names copied from the public XGN register.
openQuestions: Does e-commerce operator TDS (0.1%, the old s.194-O) apply to Luma.Green when buyers pay sellers directly, and which section of the Income-tax Act 2025 now carries it?

Are households 'consumers' under the Consumer Protection Act when they sell scrap and get a free pickup? That decides whether the E-Commerce Rules' grievance duties cover the household leg (assume yes).

Is Luma.Green an 'aggregator' for Saathi work under the Social Security Code's Seventh Schedule and the Karnataka Act if Saathis are paid by kabadiwalas, not by the platform? If so, what is the welfare fee calculated on?
What is the status of the reported 2026 Karnataka High Court challenge to the gig welfare fee?
After MeitY's January 2026 consultations, were the DPDP deadlines (about 13 May 2027) shortened for any class of company?
Have amendments to the IT Rules in 2025–26 changed the 36-hour takedown and the 24-hour / 15-day grievance timelines? The version checked was consolidated to April 2023.
Did the Finance Act 2026 enact 2% TCS on scrap? Which sellers are covered, and does the exemption for buyers who use scrap in manufacturing survive in the 2025 Act?
What penalty now applies to an unverified scale after the Jan Vishwas changes in force from 1 May 2026, and does Karnataka's enforcement rule require yearly re-verification for every instrument?
Do plain kabadiwala shops that only collect and store scrap need any KSPCB consent or authorisation under the waste rules? They are not in KSPCB's category lists.
Does Bengaluru police require scrap dealers to hold a licence or keep purchase registers?
Should the e-way bill helper use a Karnataka-specific intra-state limit, or is ₹50,000 correct for all intra-state movement? Confirm on the e-way bill portal.

result.headline: Karnataka has only 938 MW of rooftop solar, about 2.9% of India's 32.6 GW, even though KERC opened net metering to every consumer up to 1 MW in August 2026. Luma.Green's strongest solar offer is its own yards and recyclers (paybacks of about 2.5–5.5 years), not Bengaluru homes whose first 200 units are already free.

findings.point: PM Surya Ghar is now India's main rooftop solar channel. It reached 50.06 lakh households and 14.8 GW by 4 Aug 2026, and the whole process runs on one national portal.
findings.detail: PIB, 4 Aug 2026: installations rose from 5,038 a day (Oct 2025) to 16,328 a day (Jul 2026), with 5.06 lakh homes in July alone. Rs 28,024 crore of subsidy has been paid by DBT, released through PFMS in about 15 days. There are 34,219 registered vendors (29,469 active). Consumers can see vendor star ratings, and about 23,000 third-party quality inspections have been done. The portal has API links to 80+ DISCOMs, a digital net-metering agreement and DCR-portal checks. Systems up to 10 kW get deemed approval and a feasibility waiver, and 32 States/UTs dropped application and net-metering fees. On 9 Sep 2026 MNRE said the scheme was reaching 5.6 million beneficiaries, and that rooftop solar added 8.7 GW in the last year. The portal's public JS config shows its APIs sit behind consumer, vendor and DISCOM logins. A third party therefore adds value through leads and hand-holding, not through filing applications.

findings.point: The household subsidy is a fixed amount per kW, capped at 3 kW. Cheap loans are available. Businesses get no subsidy.
findings.detail: Cabinet approval, Feb 2024 (outlay Rs 75,021 crore): the central subsidy (CFA) covers 60% of benchmark cost up to 2 kW and 40% for 2–3 kW. That works out to Rs 30,000 for 1 kW, Rs 60,000 for 2 kW and Rs 78,000 for 3 kW or more. A 3 kW system averages 300+ units a month. Rajya Sabha replies, 28 Jul 2026: nationalised banks lend at repo + 50 bps, which is 5.75%, for 10 years with no collateral. 21.87 lakh loans have been sanctioned and 17.5 lakh installations were loan-financed. The FY2026-27 budget is Rs 22,000 crore, of which Rs 10,392 crore was spent by 22 Jul. The CFA is for residential consumers only. Government and commercial buildings get none because rooftop solar already pays for itself there. 12 lakh households that export power earned Rs 421 crore in FY2024-25, about Rs 3,500 each.

findings.point: Karnataka lags on rooftop solar: 938 MW of India's 32,596 MW, about 2.9%. Its regulator says small consumers have shown little interest.
findings.detail: MNRE state-wise data, 31 Aug 2026: Karnataka rooftop solar including PM Surya Ghar is 938.20 MW. Gujarat has 8,146.70 MW, Maharashtra 5,977.70 MW and Kerala 2,259.50 MW, even though Karnataka has 10,485 MW of ground-mounted solar. KERC, 25 Aug 2026: distributed solar is 920.74 MW of the state's 6,354.74 MW of solar sold under PPAs, and smaller consumers have shown little interest. BESCOM told KERC its area had 372.30 MW across 15,472 rooftop installations by Jan 2025. GESCOM reported 8,149 PM Surya Ghar applications but only 323 installed by Jan 2025, about 4% conversion. My inference on a likely cause: since Aug 2023 the state pays for 200 units a month for domestic consumers (Gruha Jyothi, noted in KERC Tariff Order 2025), so many homes have little bill left to save.

findings.point: New KERC rules for rooftop and other small solar plants (DSPV Regulations, in force 24 Aug 2026) let every consumer category use net metering up to its sanctioned load or 1,000 kW, whichever is lower. This lasts until the state reaches 3 GW, which leaves roughly 2 GW of headroom.
findings.detail:
Allowed metering types:
- Net metering.
- Net billing.
- Gross metering.
- Group net metering: same owner, minimum 5 kW, 20% of output used at the site where the plant is.
- Virtual net metering: homes, apartments, charities and government only.
- Behind-the-meter.

Hybrid inverters with batteries are allowed. A third-party owner (RESCO) can supply the plant, with no three-way agreement needed. Surplus power is bought at the KERC tariff and settled monthly; fixed and demand charges are always payable. For LT plants up to 150 kW there is no separate power-purchase agreement: the online application counts as approval, and the consumer has 150 days to finish. The DISCOM must inspect within 5 working days or the officer pays Rs 1,000 a day. Consumers with unpaid dues are not eligible. Plants under 150 kW connect to the existing transformer, and total solar on it is capped at 80% of its rating. DISCOMs must publish lists of installers, standard agreements and monthly capacity; KREDL combines these for the state. Karnataka had about 900 MW of distributed solar in Mar 2026. The Forum of Regulators' Feb 2026 model rules suggest a tighter 500 kW cap, so other states may differ.

findings.point: KERC's export tariffs and cost norms, valid 25 Aug 2026 to 30 Jun 2029, give the calculator its Karnataka numbers.
findings.detail:
All contracts run 25 years. Export tariffs:
- Domestic 1–10 kW without subsidy: Rs 3.89/kWh.
- PM Surya Ghar homes: Rs 1.96 for 1–2 kW, Rs 2.14 for >2–3 kW, Rs 2.58 above 3 kW.
- All other consumers: Rs 3.11 with domestic-content (DCR) modules, Rs 2.34 without.
- Virtual and group net metering: 75% of those rates.

Norms:
- CUF 19%, about 1,664 kWh per kW per year. Stakeholders argued for 13.5–17.5%.
- 25-year plant life, no degradation.
- Capital cost Rs 45,000/kW for homes (MNRE benchmark for 3 kW and above), Rs 27,090/kW non-DCR and Rs 36,015/kW DCR for everyone else. Module prices were Rs 13.8 vs Rs 22.3 per Wp in April 2026.
- O&M 1% of capital cost, rising 5.72% a year.
- Debt at 10.80% for 13 years.

GST on solar goods fell from 12% to 5% on 22 Sep 2025, with contracts split 70% goods and 30% services. The regulations allow grid-support charges, but none have been set; KERC had deferred them for rooftop consumers.

findings.point: BESCOM's retail tariffs set how much solar saves, and business rates changed mid-cycle in 2026.
findings.detail:
KERC Tariff Order 2025 covers FY26–FY28. Rates for FY2026-27:
- LT-1 domestic: Rs 150/kW/month plus 580 paise/kWh.
- LT-3(a) commercial: Rs 215/kW plus 680 paise.
- LT-5 industrial, which explicitly covers MSMEs and solid-waste processing plants: Rs 150/HP plus 440 paise.
- HT-2(a) industrial: Rs 350/kVA plus 660 paise. Time-of-day pricing applies to HT connections of 500 kVA and above: +100 paise 06–09 and 18–22, and −100 paise 22–06, from December to June. Solar hours are unaffected.

Domestic rooftop owners up to 10 kW get Rs 25/kW/month off fixed charges. KERC's review order of 3 Mar 2026 raised FY2025-26 rates to fund farm subsidies: LT-5 Rs 165/HP plus 520 paise, HT-2(a) Rs 365/kVA plus 670 paise, LT-3(a) Rs 235/kW plus 710 paise. The FY2026-27 rate needs checking on a live bill. BESCOM also bills an FY25 true-up of 56 paise/unit from May 2026 to Apr 2027. It is based on FY2024-25 consumption, so solar cannot avoid it. The opt-in Discounted Energy Rate Scheme (DERS: 500 paise/unit for use above base) continues for FY27–FY28, which lowers the value of solar for large business users.

findings.point: On these numbers, rooftop solar pays back in about 2–3 years for homes that pay their bill, 3–5.5 years for LT-5 yards and 2.5–3.5 years for HT recyclers. It pays back poorly for Gruha Jyothi homes on net metering.
findings.detail:
Estimates use the method in the artifact, with output of 100–138.7 kWh per kW per month and O&M at 1%.

(A) A household using 350 units a month, 3 kW system: net cost Rs 57,000 after the Rs 78,000 subsidy. Saves Rs 1,815–2,246 a month, so payback is 2.2–2.8 years; a loan EMI would be about Rs 626.

(B) A Gruha Jyothi home using 150 free units, 2 kW system: net metering saves only Rs 148–300 a month, a payback of 11–34 years. Gross metering at Rs 1.96 saves Rs 442–594, a payback of 4.8–6.8 years, if BESCOM allows it.

(C) An LT-5 yard, 15 kW non-DCR, costing Rs 4.06 lakh: payback 3.2–5.4 years (4.3–7.3 with DCR modules).

(D) An HT-2(a) recycler, 200 kW non-DCR, costing Rs 54.2 lakh: payback 2.5–3.5 years, or 3.4–4.7 years on DERS.

These are estimates, not quotes. Real prices for small systems run above the benchmark.

findings.point: Costs jump on 1 Jan 2027. From then, projects on net metering or open access must use solar cells from ALMM List-II, the government's approved list of domestic cell makers.
findings.detail: An MNRE order of 18 Jul 2026 extended the exemption from ALMM List-II for these projects from 31 May to 31 Dec 2026, and promised no further blanket extension. KERC therefore set separate tariffs for DCR and non-DCR modules; its DCR capital-cost benchmark is 33% higher (Rs 36,015 vs Rs 27,090 per kW). PM Surya Ghar already requires domestic content, checked through the DCR portal. For businesses considering solar, the next 3 months matter, and the calculator needs a DCR toggle.

findings.point: PM-KUSUM is aimed at farms and helps Luma.Green only indirectly. Its next phase adds agrivoltaics.
findings.detail:
National portal FAQ:
- Component A: 500 kW–2 MW plants on barren land, or on stilts over farm land. 25-year power-purchase agreement. DISCOMs get 40 paise/unit or Rs 6.6 lakh/MW/yr, whichever is lower, for 5 years.
- Component B: standalone solar pumps up to 7.5 HP.
- Component C: solarising grid-connected pumps, with panels up to 2x the pump's kW and surplus sold to the DISCOM.

For B and C the centre pays 30%, the state 30% and the farmer 40%; in north-eastern and hill states the centre pays 50%. MNRE, 9 Sep 2026: about 29 lakh pumps have been solarised, PM-KUSUM added 7.6 GW of decentralised solar last year, and the next phase will have a dedicated agrivoltaics component. KERC also sets benchmark tariffs for feeder-level solarisation under KUSUM Component C in Karnataka.

findings.point: Solar panels count as e-waste, but there is no EPR recycling target for them until at least 2034-35. The obligation is storage and reporting only.
Batteries are the nearer-term recycling opportunity. The rules cover every chemistry, count storage batteries as industrial, and require collectors to hand over to registered recyclers.
findings.detail:
The Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 apply to all batteries regardless of chemistry. They also apply to anyone who collects, sorts or transports waste batteries, and collectors must hand batteries to registered refurbishers or recyclers. Energy-storage batteries are classed as industrial batteries:
- Producers must collect 70% of the quantity sold three years earlier (e.g. in FY2026-27, 70% of FY2023-24 sales).
- From 2026-27, recyclers must recover 60% of material from industrial batteries and 90% from EV and portable batteries.
- From 2026-27, new industrial batteries need 40% recycled content.

EPR certificates are issued and traded on the CPCB portal. KERC's 2026 rules allow hybrid inverters with batteries, and KERC will review storage needs at 3 GW or after 2 years.

findings.point: Finance exists but is scattered across schemes: priority-sector status for loans up to Rs 35 crore, 5.75% household loans, and SIDBI green loans for MSMEs.
findings.detail: RBI Priority Sector Lending Directions 2025 (updated 11 Sep 2026): bank loans up to Rs 35 crore per borrower for renewable-energy generation, and up to Rs 10 lakh for individual households, count as priority-sector lending. PM Surya Ghar loans are 5.75% for 10 years, need no collateral, and are processed paperlessly through Jan Samarth. KERC's normative cost of business debt is 10.80% (SBI 3-year MCLR of 8.80% plus 200 bps), a fair default for business EMIs. SIDBI offers a Green Finance Scheme and an End-to-End Energy Efficiency (4E) scheme. It also runs two sub-schemes under RAMP, a World-Bank-backed MSME programme: MSE-GIFT (cheaper loans for clean and green technology) and MSE-SPICE (circular-economy investment by micro and small enterprises), which fits recyclers directly. I could not verify detailed SIDBI terms because the brochures sit behind a bot check.

findings.point: Karnataka's installers are organised and easy to find, so onboarding them as a new provider role is practical.
findings.detail: The Karnataka Renewable Energy Association (KREA) and about 48 people from installers, developers and manufacturers attended KERC's 14 Jul 2026 tariff hearing. They included CleanMax, ORB Energy, Balark Solar, Canara Solar Systems, Goldi Solar and Adani Solar. One installer put home O&M at about Rs 1,000 per cleaning. Nationally, vendors are registered and star-rated on the PM Surya Ghar portal, and KERC now requires DISCOMs to publish lists of installers. Luma.Green can check installers against those lists instead of creating its own standard.

recommendations.feature: Solar savings calculator driven by editable tariff and subsidy tables
recommendations.why: Gives investors a working solar module within days, with no external APIs. The user enters their tariff category, sanctioned load and monthly units (or the rate on their bill). The calculator returns system size in kW, a generation range, savings, payback, loan EMI, and a comparison of net and gross metering. Store every constant as a Convex row: value in paise, unit, valid-from and valid-to dates, and source URL. When KERC changes rates, as it did twice in 2026, the admin edits one row. Seed the tables with the Karnataka numbers in the artifact.

recommendations.feature: 'Your yard could save Rs X a month' card on business dashboards
recommendations.why: Luma.Green's own verified businesses are the best first buyers: LT-5 and HT-2(a) paybacks are about 2.5–5.5 years with no subsidy paperwork. Add sanctioned load and tariff category to the business profile at onboarding, fill the card from that data, and let one tap create a quote request. It is a strong demo moment because the recycling chain becomes a clean-energy customer.

recommendations.feature: Solar quote requests in the planned services module
recommendations.why: Reuses the pattern the architecture already plans (providers, requests, statuses). A request moves through: admin triage, installer assigned, site survey, quote, applied (PM Surya Ghar portal or BESCOM), installed, commissioned, subsidy received. The statuses give investors visible funnel numbers. GESCOM's 4% application-to-install conversion shows where hand-holding is worth money.

recommendations.feature: Installers as a new verified provider role, with lead routing
recommendations.why: The admin verifies GST, PM Surya Ghar vendor registration in BESCOM's area and sample installations, the same way businesses are verified today. Start with a few KREA members in Bengaluru. Charge installers, not consumers, and show every eligible installer. Consumers pick their own vendor under PM Surya Ghar, so Luma.Green must not look like it is steering them.

recommendations.feature: Plain-language application guide for each consumer type
recommendations.why: Homes: the PM Surya Ghar steps (register, pick a vendor, install, net meter, subsidy by DBT in about 15 days, 5.75% loan). Businesses: the KERC 2026 rules (no unpaid dues, automatic approval up to 150 kW, 150 days to finish, inspection within 5 days, size capped at sanctioned load or 1,000 kW). Add a banner for the 31 Dec 2026 DCR deadline and the open question on Gruha Jyothi and gross metering. It is static content in 12 languages: cheap to build and builds trust.

recommendations.feature: Old solar panels, inverters and batteries as scrap categories, with routing rules
recommendations.why: Add catalogue items: PV modules as e-waste (category CEEW14), and lead-acid and lithium batteries under the battery rules. Apply one firm rule: kabadiwalas collect and weigh but never dismantle, and yards hand over only to CPCB- or KSPCB-registered recyclers. Keep a photo, weight and handover record for each item. This fits the existing pickup flow and creates the chain-of-custody data that EPR buyers need.

recommendations.feature: Fill the calculator from a photo of the electricity bill
recommendations.why: Reuses the AI-estimate pipeline to read units, sanctioned load, tariff category and energy charge from a BESCOM bill photo. Keep only the derived numbers, never the account number or address, to stay within DPDP. Manual entry stays as a fallback. Test accuracy on real bills before users rely on it.

recommendations.feature: Group business demand for third-party-owned or bulk installs, plus finance referrals
recommendations.why: Bundle verified yards and recyclers in one industrial area into a single tender, either for third-party (RESCO) developers, which KERC allows, or for a bulk installer. Show finance options as referrals only: priority-sector bank loans up to Rs 35 crore, SIDBI GFS, 4E, MSE-GIFT and MSE-SPICE, and PM Surya Ghar loans. No lending on the platform.

recommendations.feature: Installer take-back with records ready for EPR
recommendations.why: Installers and maintenance firms book business pickups for broken panels and replaced batteries. Each record holds serial number, weight, recycler and certificate ID. These records support producers' annual PV returns now, and any PV EPR scheme after 2034-35; battery EPR certificates already trade on the CPCB portal.

recommendations.feature: Solar gigs for Saathis
recommendations.why: Add panel-cleaning and old-panel pickup jobs for trained Saathis. One installer's figure is about Rs 1,000 per home cleaning. This links to MNRE's Surya Mitra training (about 70,000 trained) and gives Saathis recurring work.

recommendations.feature: Tariff tables for every state, plus a generation log that feeds the carbon module
recommendations.why: Extend the same config tables state by state: retail tariffs, export rates and net-metering caps (the Forum of Regulators' model uses 500 kW; Karnataka uses 1,000 kW up to 3 GW). Refresh them from MNRE's monthly state-wise capacity data. Log kWh from verified business rooftops, from meter photos, to feed the planned carbon-credit module.

result.artifactMarkdown:
## Solar savings calculator: Karnataka (BESCOM) method v0, 29 Sep 2026

This gives an estimate, not a quote. Each constant is one editable config row: `key · value · unit · validFrom · validTo · sourceUrl`. Store money in paise, the unit KERC uses for energy charges.

### 1. Ask the user
| Input | Example | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Tariff category (on the bill) | LT-1 domestic · LT-3(a) commercial · LT-5 industrial · HT-2(a) industrial | Picks the tariff row |
| Sanctioned load or contract demand | 4 kW · 25 HP · 300 kVA | Caps system size; 1 HP = 0.746 kW [S3] |
| Units per month (average of recent bills) | 350 | Upper limit for units solar can offset |
| Energy charge printed on the bill (optional) | 520 paise/kWh | Overrides the defaults below, because business rates moved in 2026 (see §5) |
| Gruha Jyothi beneficiary? | yes / no | For these homes, savings come mostly from exported power |
| Module type (businesses) | DCR / non-DCR | Non-DCR modules qualify for net metering only if commissioned by 31 Dec 2026 [S7] |

### 2. Karnataka constants
| Key | Value | Valid | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Generation per kW, conservative | 100 kWh/kW/month (3 kW gives about 300 units/month) | – | [S1] |
| Generation per kW, KERC norm | 138.7 kWh/kW/month (CUF 19%) | 25.08.2026–30.06.2029 | [S5] |
| PM Surya Ghar subsidy (homes only; none for businesses) | Rs 30,000 for 1 kW · Rs 60,000 for 2 kW · Rs 78,000 for 3 kW or more (cap) | scheme period | [S1][S10] |
| Capital cost, homes 1–10 kW | Rs 45,000/kW (MNRE benchmark for 3 kW and above) | from 25.08.2026 | [S5] |
| Capital cost, businesses | Rs 27,090/kW non-DCR · Rs 36,015/kW DCR (includes 5% GST) | from 25.08.2026 | [S5] |
| Maintenance (O&M) | 1% of capital cost a year, rising 5.72% a year | same | [S5] |
| LT-1 domestic | Rs 150/kW/month + 580 paise/kWh | FY2026-27 (FY28: Rs 160 + 575) | [S3][S11] |
| LT-3(a) commercial | Rs 215/kW + 680 paise (multi-year order); FY26 reset to Rs 235 + 710 | FY27 / FY26 | [S3][S4] |
| LT-5 industrial (covers MSMEs) | Rs 150/HP + 440 paise (multi-year order); FY26 reset to Rs 165/HP + 520 | FY27 / FY26 | [S3][S4] |
| HT-2(a) industrial | Rs 350/kVA + 660 paise (multi-year order); FY26 reset to Rs 365/kVA + 670 | FY27 / FY26 | [S3][S4] |
| Discounted Energy Rate Scheme (DERS, opt-in for business connections of 50 kW and above) | 500 paise/kWh for use above base consumption | FY27–FY28 | [S3][S9] |
| Domestic rooftop rebate | Rs 25/kW/month off fixed charges (systems up to 10 kW) | FY26–FY28 | [S3] |
| Export tariff, home 1–10 kW, no subsidy | Rs 3.89/kWh (25-year contract) | 25.08.2026–30.06.2029 | [S5] |
| Export tariff, PM Surya Ghar home | Rs 1.96 (1–2 kW) · Rs 2.14 (>2–3 kW) · Rs 2.58 (>3 kW) | same | [S5] |
| Export tariff, businesses | Rs 3.11 DCR · Rs 2.34 non-DCR; virtual and group net metering get 75% of these | same | [S5] |
| Net-metering limit | Sanctioned load or 1,000 kW, whichever is lower, until the state reaches 3 GW. Systems up to 10 kW may have 10% more panel (DC) capacity | from 24.08.2026 | [S2] |
| Loans | PM Surya Ghar: 5.75%, 10 years, no collateral (up to 3 kW) · Businesses (KERC norm): 10.80%, 13 years, 70% debt / 30% equity | 2026 | [S6][S5] |

### 3. Steps
1. `kWcap` = sanctioned load in kW (HP × 0.746), no more than 1,000 kW for net metering. For homes, the subsidy stops at 3 kW.
2. `kW` = min(`kWcap`, units ÷ 100). This sizes the system to what the site can use. Round down to 0.5 kW.
3. `E` = kW × generation per kW. Show two values: low (100) and high (138.7).
4. Monthly saving:
   - **Net metering.** Units net off within the monthly bill, and surplus is paid monthly [S2].
     `min(E,U) × energyCharge + max(0,E−U) × exportTariff + rebate`
   - **Gross metering.** All generation is sold and the bill is unchanged.
     `E × exportTariff + rebate`
   - `rebate` = Rs 25 × kW for LT-1 systems up to 10 kW. Fixed and demand charges are never avoided [S2][S3].
5. `capex` = kW × benchmark (or the installer's quote). For homes, subtract the subsidy.
6. `annual` = 12 × monthly saving − O&M (1% of capex).
7. `payback` = net capex ÷ annual.
   `EMI` = P·r(1+r)^n ÷ ((1+r)^n − 1), where r = rate/12 and n = months.
8. Always show the net vs gross comparison and the low–high range, never a single promised figure.

### 4. Worked examples (this method, Karnataka numbers)
| Case | System | Net cost | Saving per month | Payback |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Home that pays its bill, LT-1, 350 units/month, 4 kW load, net metering | 3 kW | Rs 1,35,000 − 78,000 = **Rs 57,000** | Rs 1,815–2,246 | **2.2–2.8 years**; loan EMI about Rs 626 (5.75%, 10 years) |
| B. Gruha Jyothi home, 150 free units/month | 2 kW | Rs 90,000 − 60,000 = Rs 30,000 (the benchmark is for 3 kW and above; real 2 kW quotes run higher) | Net metering Rs 148–300 · gross metering Rs 442–594 | Net: 11–34 years · **gross: 4.8–6.8 years, if BESCOM allows it** |
| C. Sorting yard, LT-5, 25 HP, 2,500 units/month | 15 kW non-DCR | Rs 4.06 lakh (no subsidy) | Rs 6,600–10,816 (at 440–520 paise) | **3.2–5.4 years** (DCR: 4.3–7.3) |
| D. Plastic recycler, HT-2(a), 300 kVA, 60,000 units/month | 200 kW non-DCR | Rs 54.2 lakh | Rs 1.32–1.83 lakh (at 660 paise) | **2.5–3.5 years** (3.4–4.7 on DERS at 500 paise); EMI on 70% debt about Rs 45,300 (10.8%, 13 years) |

### 5. What changes the answer
- **Business tariffs changed mid-cycle.** KERC's review order of 3 Mar 2026 raised the FY2025-26 rates for LT-5, HT-2(a) and LT-3(a). Confirm the FY2026-27 rate from a live bill, and prefer the user's bill rate [S4].
- **Charges solar cannot avoid.** BESCOM's FY25 true-up of 56 paise/unit (May 2026–Apr 2027) is billed on FY2024-25 consumption, so solar does not reduce it [S8]. Fixed and demand charges stay too [S2].
- **Left out, so estimates are conservative.** Electricity tax and fuel/power-purchase cost adjustments scale with units used [S3]. Including them would raise savings slightly.
- **DCR deadline.** Net-metered projects commissioned after 31 Dec 2026 must use cells from ALMM List-II, the approved list of domestic cell makers. KERC's DCR capital-cost benchmark is 33% higher [S5][S7].
- **DERS.** A business on DERS pays 500 paise for extra use, so solar is worth less at the margin [S9].
- **Gruha Jyothi.** It is not verified whether a beneficiary can take gross metering and keep the 200 free units. Ask BESCOM before showing case B.
- **Site limits.** Plants under 150 kW connect to the existing transformer, and total solar on it is capped at 80% of its rating. Consumers with unpaid dues are not eligible [S2].

**Sources:**

- [S7] [PIB, ALMM List-II window to 31 Dec 2026](https://pib.gov.in/newsite/erelcontent.aspx?relid=291400)

risks: Tariffs and subsidies change often: KERC reset export tariffs on 25 Aug 2026, revised business tariffs on 3 Mar 2026, and the ALMM List-II rule starts on 1 Jan 2027. A hard-coded calculator will be wrong within months. Keep every constant as a dated, sourced config row and label outputs as estimates.
How Gruha Jyothi interacts with rooftop solar is not verified. Showing Bengaluru households a 2–3-year payback when their first 200 units are already free would mislead most of them.
Savings figures can be read as financial advice or a guarantee. Show ranges, cite sources, and state that an installer's site survey sets the real number.

Installer quality and lead fees are a risk. Bad installations damage Luma.Green's brand, and because consumers pick their own vendor under PM Surya Ghar, fees must not steer them. Charge installers, show every eligible one, and disclose any fee.
Privacy: electricity bills carry account numbers, names and addresses. Storing bill photos creates DPDP obligations, so keep only the derived numbers.

Rules may tighten. Karnataka's net metering is open only until the state reaches 3 GW; the Forum of Regulators' model rules use a 500 kW cap; and KERC may levy grid-support charges later. Any of these reduces business paybacks.

E-waste compliance: kabadiwalas dismantling panels or batteries informally would breach the E-Waste and Battery Waste rules. Storing old panels may need KSPCB authorisation, and broken modules and batteries carry safety and liability risk.
Grid and process limits can stall installs regardless of demand: the 80% transformer cap for plants under 150 kW, DISCOM delays, and unpaid dues that make consumers ineligible.
openQuestions: Can a Gruha Jyothi household install rooftop solar under gross (or net) metering and keep its 200 free units? Ask BESCOM's DSM wing.
Which LT-5 and HT-2(a) rates apply in FY2026-27 after the 3 Mar 2026 review order, which names only FY2025-26? Check a current BESCOM bill.
What does a rooftop system actually generate in Bengaluru? KERC assumes 19% CUF (about 1,664 kWh/kW/yr) while installers argued for 13.5–17.5%. Check with 5–10 real generation-meter readings.
What do Bengaluru installers charge today for 1–3 kW DCR home systems and 10–200 kW business systems, compared with the Rs 45,000, Rs 27,090 and Rs 36,015 per kW benchmarks?
Does BESCOM publish its installer list (required by KERC regulation 14.1) in a usable format? How does an installer register for PM Surya Ghar in BESCOM's area?
When will CPCB publish the PV-waste storage guideline and recovery norms that rule 12 of the E-Waste Rules refers to? Will any PV EPR target come before 2034-35?

What are the terms of MSE-GIFT and MSE-SPICE (interest subvention, capital subsidy caps), and do scrap and recycling units qualify? Get these from SIDBI directly; the brochures were behind a bot check.
Is Bengaluru one of PM Surya Ghar's 46 City Accelerator Programme cities, and could Luma.Green partner with it?
Do yards on leased land need the landlord's consent for rooftop solar, and how many pilot yards fail KERC's no-unpaid-dues rule?
